title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: "Here's Dolly for you, princess — you were so eager to see her," said Anna, coming out with Darya Alexandrovna onto the stone terrace, where Princess Varvara was sitting in the shade at an embroidery frame, working on a cover for Count Alexey Kirillovitch's easy chair. "She says she doesn't want anything before dinner, but please order her some lunch, and I'll go find Alexey and bring them all in."

Princess Varvara received Dolly cordially and rather patronizingly, and at once began to explain that she was living with Anna because she had always cared more for her than for her sister Katerina Pavlovna, the aunt who had raised Anna, and that now, when everyone else had abandoned Anna, she felt it her duty to help her through this most difficult transitional period.

"Her husband will give her a divorce, and then I shall go back to my solitude; but for now I can be useful, and I am doing my duty, however hard it is for me — unlike certain others. And how lovely of you, how right of you to have come! They live like the best of married couples; it's for God to judge them, not for us. And didn't Biryuzovsky and Madame Avenieva... and Sam Nikandrov, and Vassiliev and Madame Mamonova, and Liza Neptunova.... Did no one ever say a word about them? And it ended with all of them being received everywhere. And then, _c'est un intérieur si joli, si comme il faut. Tout-à-fait à l'anglaise. On se réunit le matin au breakfast, et puis on se sépare._ Everyone does whatever he likes until dinner. Dinner at seven. Stiva did very rightly to send you. He needs their support. You know that through his mother and his brother Alexey can do anything. And then they do so much good. Hasn't he told you about his hospital? _Ce sera admirable_ — everything from Paris."

Their conversation was cut short by Anna, who had found the men of the party in the billiard room and was coming back with them to the terrace. There was still a long time before dinner, the weather was exquisite, and several different ways of spending the next two hours were proposed. There were a great many ways to pass the time at Vozdvizhenskoe, and all of them were unlike those at Pokrovskoe.
"_Une partie de lawn-tennis_," Veslovsky proposed, with his handsome smile. "We'll be partners again, Anna Arkadyevna."
"No, it's too hot; better to stroll about the garden and take a row in the boat, and show Darya Alexandrovna the riverbanks," Vronsky proposed.
"I'm in for anything," said Sviazhsky.
"I imagine what Dolly would like best would be a walk — wouldn't you? And then the boat, perhaps," said Anna.
And so it was decided. Veslovsky and Tushkevitch went off to the bathing place, promising to ready the boat and to wait there for the others.

They walked along the path in two pairs — Anna with Sviazhsky, and Dolly with Vronsky. Dolly felt a little awkward and anxious in this new setting. In the abstract, in theory, she did not merely defend Anna's behavior; she positively approved of it. As is in fact not uncommon with women of impeccable virtue, weary of the monotony of respectable life, at a distance she had not only excused illicit love but actually envied it. Besides, she loved Anna with all her heart. But seeing Anna in real life among these strangers, in this fashionable tone so unfamiliar to her, she felt uneasy. What she particularly disliked was watching Princess Varvara ready to overlook anything for the sake of the comforts she enjoyed.

As a general principle, in the abstract, Dolly approved of Anna's choice; but to see the man for whose sake the choice had been made was unpleasant to her. Besides, she had never liked Vronsky. She thought him very proud, and saw nothing in him to be proud of except his wealth. But against her will, here in his own house, he intimidated her more than ever, and she could not be at ease with him. With him she felt the same thing she had felt with the maid about her dressing jacket. Just as with the maid she had felt not exactly ashamed, but embarrassed, by her darns, so with him she felt not exactly ashamed, but embarrassed, by herself.

Dolly felt awkward and cast about for something to talk about. Even though she supposed that, given his pride, praise of his house and garden would be sure to displease him, she told him anyway how very much she liked his house.
"Yes, it's a very fine building, and in the good old style," he said.
"I like the courtyard in front of the steps so much. Has it always been like that?"
"Oh, no!" he said, his face lighting up with pleasure. "If you could only have seen that courtyard last spring!"

And he began — at first rather diffidently, then more and more carried away by the subject — to point out to her the various details of the decoration of his house and garden. It was clear that, having put a great deal of effort into improving and beautifying his home, Vronsky felt a need to show off those improvements to someone new, and that he was genuinely delighted by Darya Alexandrovna's praise.
"If you'd care to see the hospital, and you aren't tired — it's really not far. Shall we go?" he said, glancing at her face to make sure she wasn't bored. "Are you coming, Anna?" he turned to her.
"We will, won't we?" she said, turning to Sviazhsky. "_Mais il ne faut pas laisser le pauvre Veslovsky et Tushkevitch se morfondre là dans le bateau._ We had better send someone to let them know."
"Yes, this is a monument he is putting up for himself here," Anna said, turning to Dolly with that same sly, knowing smile she had worn earlier when talking about the hospital.
"Oh, it's a real and important piece of work!" said Sviazhsky. But to show he wasn't trying to flatter Vronsky, he promptly added a few mildly critical remarks.
"Still, I do wonder, count," he said, "that while you do so much for the peasants' health, you take so little interest in the schools."

"_C'est devenu tellement commun les écoles_," said Vronsky. "You understand, it's not on principle — it just happens that my interest has been drawn elsewhere. This way to the hospital, then," he said to Darya Alexandrovna, pointing to a turning off the avenue.

The ladies put up their parasols and turned onto the side path. After several turnings, and through a small gate, Darya Alexandrovna saw, on a rise ahead of her, a large, rather pretentious red building, almost finished. The iron roof, still unpainted, glittered blindingly in the sunshine. Next to the completed building another had been begun, ringed with scaffolding. Workmen in aprons stood on the scaffolds, laying bricks, pouring mortar out of vats, and smoothing it with trowels.
"How quickly the work gets done here!" said Sviazhsky. "Last time I was here, the roof wasn't on yet."
"By autumn it will all be ready. Inside, almost everything is done," said Anna.
"And what's this new building?"

"That's where the doctor will live, and the dispensary," Vronsky said, spotting the architect in a short jacket walking up to him; and with a word of apology to the ladies, he stepped away to meet him.
Going around a pit where the workmen were slaking lime, he stopped with the architect and began to talk rather warmly.
"The front is still too low," he said to Anna, who had asked what the matter was.
"I said the foundation ought to have been raised," said Anna.
"Yes, of course it would have been much better, Anna Arkadyevna," the architect said, "but now it is too late."

"Yes, I take a great interest in it," Anna said in answer to Sviazhsky, who was expressing his surprise at her grasp of architecture. "This new building should have been in keeping with the hospital. It was an afterthought, and was begun without a plan."
Having finished his talk with the architect, Vronsky rejoined the ladies and led them into the hospital.

Although the cornices outside were still being worked on and the ground floor was being painted, upstairs almost all of the rooms were finished. Going up the broad cast-iron staircase to the landing, they walked into the first large room. The walls were stuccoed to look like marble; the huge plate-glass windows were already in; only the parquet floor was still unfinished, and the carpenters, who had been planing a block of it, left their work, took off the bands that tied back their hair, and bowed to the gentry.
"This is the reception room," Vronsky said. "There will be a desk in here, some tables, and benches, and nothing more."
"This way; let's go in here. Don't go near the window," said Anna, touching the paint to see whether it was dry. "Alexey, the paint's dry already," she added.

From the reception room they went into the corridor. Here Vronsky showed them the ventilation system, which was of a new pattern. Then he showed them the marble baths and beds with extraordinary springs. Then he took them through the wards one by one, the storeroom, the linen room, and then the heating stove of a new design, and the trolleys that would carry everything needed silently along the corridors, and many other things besides. Sviazhsky, a connoisseur of the latest mechanical improvements, took it all in with appreciation. Dolly simply marveled at all she had never seen before, and, anxious to understand it all, asked detailed questions about everything, to Vronsky's great satisfaction.
"Yes, I imagine this will be the only properly equipped hospital in Russia," said Sviazhsky.
"And aren't you going to have a maternity ward?" Dolly asked. "That's so badly needed in the country. I have so often...."
Despite his usual courtesy, Vronsky cut her off.

"This is not a maternity home, but a hospital for the sick, and it's meant for all conditions, except contagious ones," he said. "Ah! look at this," and he rolled an invalid chair, just ordered for convalescents, over to Darya Alexandrovna. "Look." He sat down in it and started moving it. "The patient can't walk — still too weak, perhaps, or with something wrong with his legs — but he needs air, and so he can move himself, roll himself along...."

Darya Alexandrovna was interested by it all. She liked everything very much, but most of all she liked Vronsky himself, with his natural, simple-hearted enthusiasm. "Yes, he's a very nice, good man," she thought several times, not hearing what he said but watching him and taking in his expression, while she mentally put herself in Anna's place. She liked him so much, just then, with his eager interest, that she saw how Anna could be in love with him.

title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: "No, I think the princess is tired, and horses don't interest her," Vronsky said to Anna, who had wanted to go on to the stables, where Sviazhsky wished to see the new stallion. "You go ahead, while I walk the princess back home, and we can have a little talk — if you would like that?" he added, turning to Dolly.
"I know nothing about horses, and I would be delighted," Darya Alexandrovna answered, rather astonished.

She could see from Vronsky's face that he wanted something from her. She was not mistaken. As soon as they had gone back through the little gate into the garden, he looked in the direction Anna had taken, and once he had made sure she could neither hear nor see them, he began:

"You can guess that I have something I want to say to you," he said, looking at her with laughing eyes. "I am not wrong, am I, in thinking of you as Anna's friend." He took off his hat, drew out his handkerchief, and wiped his head, which was growing bald.
Darya Alexandrovna made no answer and only stared at him, alarmed. Left alone with him, she suddenly felt afraid; his laughing eyes and stern expression frightened her.

The most varied suppositions of what he was about to bring up flashed through her mind. "He's going to beg me to come and stay with them with the children, and I'll have to refuse; or to put together a set that will receive Anna in Moscow.... Or is it about Vassenka Veslovsky and his way with Anna? Or perhaps about Kitty — that he feels he was to blame?" All her guesses were unpleasant, and none of them was right.
"You have so much influence with Anna; she is so fond of you," he said. "Help me."

Darya Alexandrovna looked with timid inquiry into his eager face, which, under the lime trees, was alternately lit up in patches by the sun and then dropped back into deep shadow. She waited for him to say more, but he walked beside her in silence, scratching at the gravel with his cane.

"You have come to see us — you, the only one of Anna's former friends, I'm not counting Princess Varvara — but I know you have not come because you consider our position normal, but because, understanding the whole difficulty of it, you still love her and want to help her. Have I understood you rightly?" he asked, glancing at her.
"Oh, yes," answered Darya Alexandrovna, lowering her parasol, "but...."

"No," he interrupted, and, oblivious of the awkwardness it caused her, he stopped abruptly, so that she had to stop short too. "No one feels more deeply or intensely than I do all the difficulty of Anna's position; and you may readily understand that, if you do me the honor of supposing I have any heart at all. I am the one to blame for that position, and that is why I feel it."

"I understand," said Darya Alexandrovna, involuntarily admiring the sincerity and force with which he said it. "But just because you feel responsible, you exaggerate it, I am afraid," she said. "Her position in society is difficult, I can well believe."
"In society it is hell!" he brought out quickly, scowling. "You cannot imagine the moral suffering she endured in those two weeks in Petersburg — and I beg you to take my word for it."
"Yes, but here, so long as neither Anna — nor you — feel the absence of society...."
"Society!" he said contemptuously. "How could I miss society?"

"So far — and perhaps always — you are happy and at peace. I can see in Anna that she is happy, completely happy; she has already managed to tell me so many times," Darya Alexandrovna said, smiling; and as she said it, at the very same moment, a doubt entered her mind whether Anna really was happy.
But Vronsky, it seemed, had no doubts on that score.

"Yes, yes," he said. "I know she has revived after all her suffering. She is happy. She is happy in the present. But I?... I'm afraid of what is ahead of us.... Forgive me — would you like to walk on?"
"No, I don't mind."
"Well, then, let's sit here."
Darya Alexandrovna sat down on a garden seat in a corner of the avenue. He stood facing her.

"I can see that she is happy," he repeated, and the doubt whether she really was happy sank deeper into Darya Alexandrovna's mind. "But can it last? Whether we acted rightly or wrongly is another question, but the die is cast," he said, slipping from Russian into French, "and we are bound together for life. We are joined by all the ties of love that we hold most sacred. We have a child; we may have other children. But the law, and all the conditions of our position, are such that thousands of complications arise which she does not see and does not want to see. And that one can understand. But I cannot help seeing them. My daughter, by law, is not my daughter — she is Karenin's. I cannot endure that lie!" he said, with a sharp gesture of refusal, and he looked toward Darya Alexandrovna with grim inquiry.
She made no answer; she only gazed at him. He went on:

"One day a son may be born — my son — and by law he will be a Karenin. He will not be the heir of my name or of my property, and however happy we may be in our home life and however many children we may have, there will be no real bond between us. They will be Karenins. You can understand the bitterness and horror of this situation! I have tried to talk about it to Anna. It irritates her. She doesn't understand, and to her I cannot speak openly about all of this. Now look at it from another side. I am happy, happy in her love, but I have to have something to do. I have found that occupation, and I am proud of what I am doing and consider it nobler than the pursuits of my former companions at court and in the army. And I would certainly not exchange my work for theirs. I am working here, settled in my own place, and I am happy and content, and we need nothing more in order to be happy. I love my work here. _Ce n'est pas un pis-aller_; on the contrary...."

Darya Alexandrovna noticed that at this point in his explanation he grew muddled, and she did not quite follow the digression, but she sensed that, having once started talking about matters close to his heart that he could not speak of to Anna, he was now making a clean breast of everything, and that the question of his pursuits in the country belonged to the same category — matters close to his heart — as the question of his relations with Anna.

"Well, I'll go on," he said, collecting himself. "The main thing is that, as I work, I need to be sure that what I am doing won't die with me, that I shall have heirs after me — and this I do not have. Imagine the situation of a man who knows his children, the children of the woman he loves, will not be his, but will belong to someone who hates them and cares nothing for them! It is unbearable!"
He paused, clearly very moved.
"Yes, indeed, I see that. But what can Anna do?" Darya Alexandrovna asked.

"Yes, and that brings me to what I really wanted to talk to you about," he said, calming himself with an effort. "Anna can — it depends on her.... Even to petition the Tsar for legitimization, a divorce is essential. And that depends on Anna. Her husband agreed to a divorce — at that point, your husband had arranged everything. And now, I know, he would not refuse it. It is only a matter of writing to him. He said plainly at the time that if she expressed the wish, he would not refuse. Of course," he said gloomily, "it is one of those Pharisaical cruelties only such heartless men are capable of. He knows what agony any memory of him must cause her, and knowing her, he still requires a letter from her. I can understand that it is agony for her. But the matter is so important that one must _passer par-dessus toutes ces finesses de sentiment. Il y va du bonheur et de l'existence d'Anne et de ses enfants._ I won't speak of myself, though it is hard for me, very hard," he said, with a look as if he were threatening someone over how hard it was for him. "And so, princess, I am shamelessly clutching at you as an anchor of salvation. Help me persuade her to write to him and ask for a divorce."
"Yes, of course," Darya Alexandrovna said dreamily, vividly recalling her last conversation with Alexey Alexandrovitch. "Yes, of course," she repeated firmly, thinking of Anna.
"Use your influence on her, get her to write. I don't want to — I almost can't — speak about this to her."

"Very well, I will talk to her. But how is it she does not think of it herself?" said Darya Alexandrovna, and for some reason at that very moment she remembered Anna's strange new habit of half-closing her eyes. And she remembered that Anna dropped her lids exactly when the deeper questions of life came up. "As if she half shuts her eyes to her own life, so as not to see all of it," Dolly thought. "Yes, indeed, for my own sake and for hers, I will speak to her," Dolly said in reply to his look of gratitude.
They got up and walked back to the house.

title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: When Anna found Dolly home before her, she looked intently into her eyes, as if asking about the talk she had had with Vronsky, but in words she asked nothing.
"It must be dinnertime," she said. "We've not had any time to ourselves yet. I'm counting on the evening. Now I want to go and change. I expect you do too — we all got splashed at the building site."

Dolly went to her room and was amused by the situation. There was no way to change her dress; she had already put on her best one. But to mark her preparations for dinner somehow, she asked the maid to brush her dress, changed her cuffs and tie, and put some lace on her head.
"This is all I can manage," she said with a smile to Anna, who came in wearing yet a third dress, again of the utmost simplicity.

"Yes, we are too formal here," Anna said, as if apologizing for her magnificence. "Alexey is delighted at your visit — he rarely is at anything. He has completely lost his heart to you," she added. "You're not tired?"

There was no time to talk about anything before dinner. Going into the drawing room, they found Princess Varvara already there, and the gentlemen of the party in black frock coats. The architect wore a swallow-tail coat. Vronsky introduced the doctor and the steward to his guest; the architect he had already presented to her at the hospital.

A stout butler, resplendent with a smoothly shaven round chin and a starched white cravat, announced that dinner was ready, and the ladies got up. Vronsky asked Sviazhsky to take Anna Arkadyevna in, and offered his own arm to Dolly. Veslovsky beat Tushkevitch to it in offering his arm to Princess Varvara, so that Tushkevitch went in alone with the steward and the doctor.

The dinner, the dining room, the table service, the waiting at table, the wine, and the food were not only in keeping with the general tone of modern luxury throughout the house — they seemed even more sumptuous and modern. Darya Alexandrovna watched this luxury, which was new to her, and as a good housekeeper used to running a household — even though she never dreamed of adapting any of what she saw to her own household, since it was all in a style of luxury far beyond her own way of living — she could not help studying every detail and asking herself how and by whom it was all done. Vassenka Veslovsky, her husband, even Sviazhsky, and many other people she knew, would never have raised such a question, and would have happily accepted what every well-bred host tries to make his guests believe — that everything well-ordered in his house has cost him, the host, no trouble at all, but comes of itself. Darya Alexandrovna knew very well that even porridge for the children's breakfast does not come of itself, and that therefore, where so elaborate and grand a style of luxury was maintained, someone had to be giving it serious attention. And from the way Alexey Kirillovitch scanned the table, the way he nodded to the butler, and the way he offered Darya Alexandrovna her choice between cold and hot soup, she saw that it was all arranged and kept up by the care of the master of the house himself. It was obvious that it rested no more on Anna than on Veslovsky. She, Sviazhsky, the princess, and Veslovsky were equally guests, lightheartedly enjoying what had been laid on for them.

Anna was the hostess only in the matter of directing the conversation. And the conversation was a difficult one for the lady of the house at a small table with people present, such as the steward and the architect, from a completely different world, struggling not to be overawed by an elegance they were not used to, and unable to carry a large share of the general talk. But this difficult conversation Anna directed with her usual tact and naturalness, and indeed she did so with actual enjoyment, as Darya Alexandrovna noticed. The talk began with the row Tushkevitch and Veslovsky had taken alone together in the boat, and Tushkevitch began describing the latest boat races at the Petersburg Yacht Club. But Anna, seizing the first pause, turned to the architect at once, to draw him out of his silence.

"Nikolay Ivanitch was struck," she said, meaning Sviazhsky, "at how the new building has progressed since the last time he was here; but I'm there every day, and every day I am amazed at how quickly it goes up."

"It's first-rate working for his excellency," said the architect with a smile (he was respectful and self-possessed, with a quiet sense of his own dignity). "It's a very different matter from dealing with district authorities. Where you would have to fill out reams of paper, here I just call on the count, and we settle the business in three words."
"The American way of doing business," Sviazhsky said with a smile.
"Yes, over there they build sensibly...."
The conversation turned to the misuse of political power in the United States, but Anna quickly steered it onto another subject, so as to draw the steward into the talk.
"Have you ever seen a reaping machine?" she said to Darya Alexandrovna. "We had just ridden over to look at one when we ran into you. It was the first time I had ever seen one."
"How do they work?" Dolly asked.
"Exactly like little scissors. A plank, and a row of little scissors. Like this."

Anna took up a knife and fork in her beautiful white, ring-covered hands and began demonstrating how the machine worked. It was clear that she saw nothing would be made clear by her demonstration; but, aware that her talk was pleasing and her hands beautiful, she kept on explaining.
"More like little penknives," Veslovsky said playfully, his eyes never leaving her.
Anna gave a barely perceptible smile but made no reply. "Isn't it true, Karl Fedoritch — it's just like little scissors?" she said to the steward.
"_Oh, ja_," the German answered. _"Es ist ein ganz einfaches Ding,"_ and he began to explain the way the machine was built.
"It's a shame it doesn't bind too. I saw one at the Vienna exhibition that binds with wire," said Sviazhsky. "Those would be more profitable to use."

_"Es kommt drauf an.... Der Preis vom Draht muss ausgerechnet werden."_ And the German, his silence broken, turned to Vronsky. _"Das lässt sich ausrechnen, Erlaucht."_ The German was already feeling in the pocket where he kept his pencil and the notebook he always wrote in, but, remembering that he was at a dinner table and noticing Vronsky's chilly glance, he checked himself. _"Zu compliziert, macht zu viel Klopot,"_ he concluded.
_"Wünscht man Dochots, so hat man auch Klopots,"_ said Vassenka Veslovsky, mimicking the German. _"J'adore l'allemand,"_ he added, turning to Anna again with the same smile.
_"Cessez,"_ she said, with playful severity.
"We expected to find you in the fields, Vassily Semyonitch," she said to the doctor, a sickly-looking man. "Did you go?"
"I went, but I took flight," the doctor answered with grim jocularity.
"So you got a good walk?"
"Splendid!"
"And how was the old woman? I hope it's not typhus?"
"Typhus, no — but it is taking a bad turn."
"What a pity!" said Anna, and, having paid the dues of civility to her own circle, she turned back to her own friends.
"It would still be a hard task to build a machine from your description, Anna Arkadyevna," Sviazhsky said jokingly.

"Oh, no — why?" said Anna, with a smile that betrayed she knew there was something charming in her disquisition on the machine, something Sviazhsky had noticed. This new touch of girlish coquettishness made an unpleasant impression on Dolly.
"But Anna Arkadyevna's grasp of architecture is marvelous," said Tushkevitch.
"Indeed, I heard Anna Arkadyevna yesterday talking about plinths and damp-courses," said Veslovsky. "Have I got the words right?"
"It's hardly marvelous when you live around it and hear about it constantly," said Anna. "Though I'll bet you don't even know what houses are built out of?"
Darya Alexandrovna could see that Anna disliked the tone of teasing that ran between herself and Veslovsky, and yet kept slipping into it in spite of herself.
Vronsky's behavior in this matter was completely unlike Levin's. He clearly attached no importance to Veslovsky's chatter; on the contrary, he encouraged his jokes.
"Come now, Veslovsky, tell us — how are the stones held together?"
"By cement, of course."
"Bravo! And what is cement?"
"Oh, some sort of paste... no, putty," said Veslovsky, raising a general laugh.

The company at dinner, with the exception of the doctor, the architect, and the steward, who stayed locked in gloomy silence, kept up a conversation that never paused, glancing off one subject and fastening on another, and now and then stinging one or another to the quick. At one point Darya Alexandrovna felt cut to the quick herself, and grew so hot that she actually flushed, and afterwards wondered whether she had said anything too sharp or out of turn. Sviazhsky started talking about Levin, describing his odd view that machinery was simply harmful in its effect on Russian agriculture.

"I have not the pleasure of knowing this Monsieur Levin," Vronsky said, smiling, "but most likely he has never seen the machines he condemns; or if he has seen and tried any, he must have done so in some odd way, with some Russian imitation, not a real machine from abroad. What sort of view can anyone have on such a subject?"
"Turkish views, generally speaking," Veslovsky said, turning to Anna with a smile.

"I can't defend his opinions," Darya Alexandrovna said, firing up. "But I can say that he is a highly cultivated man, and if he were here, he would know very well how to answer you, though I am not capable of doing so."

"I like him very much, and we are great friends," Sviazhsky said, smiling good-naturedly. "_Mais pardon, il est un petit peu toqué_; he maintains, for example, that the district councils and the arbitration boards are all of no use, and he refuses to take any part in any of it."

"It is our Russian apathy," Vronsky said, pouring water from an iced decanter into a fine glass on a high stem. "We've no sense of the duties our privileges impose on us, and so we refuse to recognize those duties."
"I know no man more conscientious in the discharge of his duties," Darya Alexandrovna said, irritated by Vronsky's tone of superiority.

"As for me," Vronsky went on, evidently for some reason keenly stirred by this conversation, "such as I am, on the contrary, I am extremely grateful for the honor they have done me — thanks to Nikolay Ivanitch" (he indicated Sviazhsky) — "in electing me a justice of the peace. I consider that, for me, the duty of being present at the session, of judging some peasants' quarrel about a horse, is as important as anything else I can do. And I shall regard it as an honor if they elect me to the district council. It is only in that way that I can pay back what I enjoy as a landowner. Unfortunately people do not understand the weight that the great landowners ought to carry in the state."

It was strange to Darya Alexandrovna to hear how serenely certain he was of being right at his own table. She thought of how Levin, who held the opposite view, was just as positive in his opinions at his own table. But she loved Levin, and so she was on his side.

"So can we count on you for the coming elections, count?" said Sviazhsky. "But you must come down a little early, so as to be on the spot by the eighth. If you would do me the honor of staying with me."

"I rather agree with your _beau-frère_," said Anna, "though not quite on his grounds," she added, smiling. "I'm afraid we have too many of these public duties nowadays. Just as in the old days there were so many government officials that you had to call in an official for every little thing, so now everybody is doing some sort of public service. Alexey has been here six months, and I believe he is already a member of five or six different bodies. _Du train que cela va_, the whole of life will go on it. And I am afraid that with such a multiplication of these bodies, they'll all end up as mere form. How many are you a member of, Nikolay Ivanitch?" she turned to Sviazhsky. "Over twenty, I think."

Anna spoke lightly, but irritation could be heard in her tone. Darya Alexandrovna, watching Anna and Vronsky closely, caught it at once. She noticed too that as Anna spoke, Vronsky's face had immediately taken on a serious, stubborn look. Noticing that, and Princess Varvara hurrying in to change the subject by talking of Petersburg acquaintances, and remembering what Vronsky had said, apparently out of nowhere, in the garden, about his work in the country, Dolly guessed that this question of public activity was tied to some deep private disagreement between Anna and Vronsky.

The dinner, the wine, the table decoration were all very good; but it was all like what Darya Alexandrovna had seen at formal dinners and balls — which in recent years had become quite unfamiliar to her — it all had the same impersonal, constrained character, and so, on an ordinary day in a small circle of friends, it made an unpleasant impression on her.

After dinner they sat on the terrace for a while, then went on to play lawn tennis. The players, split into two parties, took up positions on either side of a tightly drawn net with gilt poles on the carefully leveled and rolled croquet ground. Darya Alexandrovna tried to play, but it took her a long time to grasp the game, and by the time she did, she was so tired that she sat down beside Princess Varvara and simply watched the rest. Her partner, Tushkevitch, gave up too, but the others kept the game going for a long time. Sviazhsky and Vronsky both played very well and seriously. They kept a sharp eye on the balls served to them, and without hurrying or getting in each other's way, they ran up to them deftly, waited for the bounce, and returned them cleanly and accurately over the net. Veslovsky played worse than the others. He was too eager, but he kept the players lively with his high spirits. His laughter and shouting never stopped. Like the other men of the party, with the ladies' permission, he took off his coat, and his solid, handsome figure in his white shirtsleeves, with his red sweating face and his impulsive movements, made a picture that printed itself vividly on the memory.
When Darya Alexandrovna lay in bed that night, as soon as she shut her eyes, she saw Vassenka Veslovsky flying about the croquet ground.

During the game Darya Alexandrovna had not been enjoying herself. She did not like the light, bantering tone that was kept up the whole time between Vassenka Veslovsky and Anna, and the general unnaturalness of grown-ups, all alone without children, playing a children's game. But, to avoid breaking up the party and to fill the time somehow, she joined the game again after a rest and pretended to be enjoying it. All that day it felt to her as though she were acting in a play with actors cleverer than she was, and that her bad acting was spoiling the whole performance. She had come intending to stay two days, if all went well. But that evening, during the game, she made up her mind to go home the next day. The maternal cares and worries she had so hated on the way out now, after a day without them, struck her in a quite different light, and drew her back to them.

When, after evening tea and a row on the river by night, Darya Alexandrovna went alone to her room, took off her dress, and began arranging her thin hair for the night, she felt a great sense of relief.
It was positively unpleasant to her to think that Anna was about to come in to see her. She longed to be alone with her own thoughts.

title: Chapter 23
paragraphs: Dolly was about to go to bed when Anna came in to see her, dressed for the night. Several times during the day Anna had begun to speak of things near her heart, and every time, after a few words, she had stopped: "Later — when we're by ourselves, we'll talk about everything. I have so much to tell you," she had said.

Now they were by themselves, and Anna did not know what to say. She sat at the window looking at Dolly and ran through, in her own mind, all the stores of intimate talk that had seemed so inexhaustible beforehand, and found nothing. At that moment it felt to her that everything had already been said.
"Well, what about Kitty?" she said with a heavy sigh, looking penitently at Dolly. "Tell me the truth, Dolly: isn't she angry with me?"
"Angry? Oh, no!" said Darya Alexandrovna, smiling.
"But she hates me, despises me?"
"Oh, no! But you know that sort of thing isn't forgiven."

"Yes, yes," Anna said, turning away and looking out of the open window. "But it was not my fault. And whose fault was it? What does fault even mean? Could it have been otherwise? What do you think? Could it possibly have been that you didn't become Stiva's wife?"
"Really, I don't know. But this is what I want you to tell me...."
"Yes, yes, but we haven't finished with Kitty. Is she happy? They say he is a very nice man."
"He is much more than very nice. I don't know a better man."
"Ah, how glad I am! I'm so glad! Much more than very nice," she repeated.
Dolly smiled.
"But tell me about yourself. We have so much to talk about. And I have had a talk with...." Dolly did not know what to call him. She felt awkward calling him either the count or Alexey Kirillovitch.
"With Alexey," said Anna. "I know what you talked about. But I want to ask you straight out — what do you think of me, of my life?"
"How can I say it like that, just like that? I really don't know."

"No, tell me all the same.... You see my life. But you mustn't forget that you're seeing us in the summer, when you have come and we are not alone.... We came here in the early spring, and lived completely alone, and we will be alone again, and I want nothing better. But imagine me living alone, without him, alone — and that's what it will come to. I can see by everything that it will be the case often enough, that he will be away from home half the time," she said, getting up and sitting down close beside Dolly.

"Of course," she went on, cutting off Dolly, who was about to answer, "of course I won't try to keep him by force. I don't keep him as it is. The races are coming, his horses are running, and he will go. I'm very glad. But think of me — imagine my position.... Still, what's the use of talking about it?" She smiled. "Well, what did he talk to you about?"

"He talked about what I myself want to talk about, and so it's easy for me to be his advocate: about whether there isn't a possibility... whether you couldn't...." (Darya Alexandrovna hesitated) "...correct, improve, your position.... You know how I look at it.... But all the same, if it is possible, you should get married...."

"You mean a divorce?" said Anna. "Do you know, the only woman who came to see me in Petersburg was Betsy Tverskaya? You know her, of course. _Au fond, c'est la femme la plus dépravée qui existe._ She had an affair with Tushkevitch, deceiving her husband in the basest way. And she told me she didn't care to know me as long as my position was irregular. Don't imagine I would compare.... I know you, darling. But I couldn't help remembering.... Well — so what did he say to you?" she repeated.

"He said he is unhappy on your account and on his own. Perhaps you'll say it's egoism, but what a legitimate, noble egoism it is. He wants, first and foremost, to legitimize his daughter, and to be your husband, to have a legal right to you."
"What wife, what slave, can be more utterly a slave than I am in my position?" she put in gloomily.
"The main thing he wants... is for you not to suffer."
"That's impossible. Well?"
"Well, and the most legitimate wish — he wants your children to have a name."
"What children?" said Anna, not looking at Dolly and half-closing her eyes.
"Annie and any to come...."
"He needn't worry about that. I shall have no more children."
"How can you say you won't?"
"I will not, because I don't wish to." And, for all her emotion, Anna smiled when she saw the naïve mix of curiosity, astonishment, and horror cross Dolly's face.
"The doctor told me after my illness...."
"Impossible!" said Dolly, her eyes opening wide.

For her this was one of those revelations whose consequences and implications are so enormous that the first reaction is the sense that it is impossible to take in, and that one will have to think about it a very great deal.

This revelation, suddenly throwing light on all those families of one or two children that had been incomprehensible to her until now, stirred up so many thoughts, reflections, and contradictory feelings that she had nothing to say and simply stared at Anna with wide-open, wondering eyes. This was the very thing she had been dreaming of, but now, learning that it was possible, she was horrified. She felt it was too simple a solution to too complicated a problem.
_"N'est-ce pas immoral?"_ was all she said, after a short pause.

"Why so? Think — I have a choice between two alternatives: either to be with child, that is, an invalid, or to be the friend and companion of my husband — practically my husband," Anna said in a tone deliberately light and frivolous.
"Yes, yes," said Darya Alexandrovna, hearing the very arguments she had used on herself, and no longer finding the same force in them as before.

"For you, for other people," said Anna, as if reading her thoughts, "there may be room to hesitate; but for me.... You have to remember — I am not his wife; he loves me as long as he loves me. And how am I to keep his love? Not by being like this!"

She swept her white hands in a curve in front of her waist with extraordinary speed, as people do in moments of excitement. Ideas and memories rushed through Darya Alexandrovna's mind. "I," she thought, "didn't keep my attraction for Stiva; he left me for others, and the first woman he betrayed me with didn't keep him by being always pretty and lively. He left her and took up with another. And can Anna attract and keep Count Vronsky that way? If that is what he is after, he will find dresses and manners still more attractive and charming. And however white and beautiful her bare arms are, however lovely her full figure and her eager face under her black curls, he will find something better still — just as my disgusting, pitiful, charming husband always does."
Dolly made no answer; she only sighed. Anna caught the sigh as a sign of disagreement and went on. In her armory she had other arguments so strong that there was no answering them.

"You say it isn't right? But you have to think," she went on. "You forget my position. How can I want children? I am not talking about the suffering; I'm not afraid of that. Think only — what would my children be? Ill-fated children, who would carry a stranger's name. By the very fact of their birth they would be forced to be ashamed of their mother, of their father, of their own birth."
"But that is exactly why a divorce is necessary." But Anna did not hear her. She was longing to give voice to all the arguments with which she had convinced herself so many times before.
"Why have I been given reason at all, if not to use it to avoid bringing unhappy creatures into the world?" She looked over at Dolly, but did not wait for an answer:
"I would always feel I had wronged those unhappy children," she said. "If they don't exist, at least they aren't unhappy; while if they are unhappy, I alone would be to blame for it."

These were arguments Darya Alexandrovna had run through in her own head; but now, hearing them spoken aloud, she couldn't really take them in. "How can you wrong creatures who don't exist?" she thought. And then it hit her all at once: could it conceivably, under any circumstances at all, have been better for her favorite Grisha if he had never been born? The idea felt so wild, so monstrous, that she shook her head to clear out the tangle of whirling, half-mad thoughts.
"No, I don't know — it isn't right," was all she said, with an expression of disgust on her face.

"Yes, but you mustn't forget that you and I.... And besides that," added Anna, in spite of the wealth of her arguments and the poverty of Dolly's objections, still seeming to admit that it was not right, "don't forget the main point — that I am not in the same position as you. For you the question is: do you want any more children? For me, it is: do I want any at all? And that's a big difference. You must see that I can't want it in my position."

Darya Alexandrovna made no reply. She suddenly felt that she had moved far away from Anna; that between them there lay a barrier of questions on which they could never agree, and which it was better not to speak of.

title: Chapter 24
paragraphs: "Then there's all the more reason to legalize your position, if you can," Dolly said.
"Yes, if I can," Anna said, suddenly in a completely different register — subdued, mournful.
"Surely a divorce isn't out of the question? I was told your husband had agreed to it."
"Dolly, I don't want to talk about that."
"All right, we won't," Darya Alexandrovna said quickly, noticing the look of pain that crossed Anna's face. "All I'm saying is that you take too dark a view of things."
"Me? Not at all! I'm always cheerful and happy. You see — _je fais des passions._ Veslovsky…"
"Honestly, I don't much like Veslovsky's tone," Darya Alexandrovna said, eager to change the subject.

"Oh, nonsense! He amuses Alexey, that's all — he's a boy, completely under my thumb. You know, I steer him wherever I want. Just as you'd handle your Grisha.… Dolly!" — she switched abruptly — "you say I take too dark a view of things. You can't understand. It's too awful! I try not to take any view of it at all."
"But I think you should. You ought to do whatever you can."

"What can I do? Nothing. You tell me to marry Alexey, and you say I don't think about it. I don't think about it!" she repeated, the color rising in her face. She got up, straightened her back, and let out a heavy sigh. With her light step she began pacing the room, stopping now and then. "I don't think of it? Not a day, not an hour goes by that I don't think of it, and blame myself for thinking of it — because thinking of it could drive me mad. Drive me mad!" she repeated. "When I think of it I can't sleep without morphine. But never mind. Let's talk calmly. They tell me — divorce. First of all, he won't give me one. He's under the influence of Countess Lidia Ivanovna now."
Darya Alexandrovna, sitting straight on her chair, turned her head, her face following Anna with sympathetic pain.
"You ought to make the attempt," she said softly.

"Suppose I make the attempt. What does it actually mean?" Anna said, plainly giving voice to a thought she had rehearsed a thousand times. "It means that I, hating him, but still admitting that I've wronged him — and I do consider him magnanimous — humiliate myself by writing to him.… All right, suppose I make the effort; I do it. Either I get a humiliating refusal or I get his consent.… Fine, say I have his consent.…" Anna was at the far end of the room now, and she stopped there, fiddling with the curtain at the window. "I have his consent. But my… my son? They won't give him to me. He'll grow up despising me, with his father — the man I abandoned. Do you understand? I love them equally, I think, but both of them more than myself — two creatures, Seryozha and Alexey."

She walked back to the middle of the room and stood facing Dolly, her arms pressed tightly across her chest. In her white dressing gown her figure looked grander and broader than usual. She bent her head and, with shining wet eyes, looked from under her brows at Dolly — a thin, pitiful little figure in a patched dressing jacket and nightcap, trembling all over with emotion.

"It's only those two creatures that I love, and one excludes the other. I can't have them together, and that's the only thing I want. And since I can't have it, nothing else matters to me. Nothing at all. It will end one way or another, and that's why I can't bear to talk about it. So don't blame me, don't judge me for any of it. You can't, with your pure heart, understand everything I'm going through." She went over, sat down beside Dolly, and, with a guilty look, glanced into her face and took her hand.

"What are you thinking? What are you thinking about me? Don't despise me. I don't deserve contempt. I'm simply unhappy. If anyone is unhappy, I am," she got out, and turning away, she burst into tears.

Left alone, Darya Alexandrovna said her prayers and went to bed. While Anna had been speaking she'd felt for her with all her heart, but now she couldn't make herself keep thinking about her. The memory of home and of her children rose in her imagination with a peculiar charm — quite new to her — a kind of fresh brilliance. That world of her own seemed so sweet and precious now that nothing could persuade her to spend one extra day outside it, and she made up her mind to head back the next day for certain.

Meanwhile Anna went back to her boudoir, picked up a wine-glass and let several drops of a medicine fall into it — the active ingredient being morphine. After drinking it off and sitting still for a little while, she went into her bedroom feeling soothed and in better spirits.

When she came in, Vronsky studied her closely. He was searching for traces of the conversation he knew she must have had with Dolly, having spent so long in her room. But in her expression — that contained excitement, that air of holding something in reserve — he could find nothing but the beauty that always cast its fresh spell on him, though he was used to it, the consciousness of that beauty, and the desire that it should work on him. He didn't want to ask what they had been talking about, but he hoped she'd offer him something of her own accord. All she said was:
"I'm so glad you like Dolly. You do, don't you?"
"Oh, I've known her a long time, you know. She's very good-hearted, I suppose, _mais excessivement terre-à-terre._ Still, I'm very glad to see her."
He took Anna's hand and looked questioningly into her eyes.

Misreading the look, she smiled at him. The next morning, despite her hosts' protests, Darya Alexandrovna got ready for the trip home. Levin's coachman, in his far-from-new coat and shabby hat, with his ill-matched horses and his carriage with the patched mudguards, drove with grim determination into the covered gravel forecourt.

Darya Alexandrovna disliked saying goodbye to Princess Varvara and the gentlemen of the party. After a day together, both she and her hosts were perfectly clear that they did not get on, and that it was better not to meet again. Only Anna was sad. She knew that with Dolly gone, no one would stir up in her again the feelings their conversation had stirred. It hurt to disturb those feelings, but she also knew it was the best part of her soul, and that this part of her would soon be smothered by the life she was leading.

Once they were out in the open country, Darya Alexandrovna felt a delicious sense of release, and she was tempted to ask the two men how they had liked being at Vronsky's, when suddenly the coachman, Philip, spoke up on his own:

"Rolling in money they may be, but three pots of oats is all we got. Cleaned out down to the last grain before the cocks crowed. What's three pots? A mouthful! And oats are down to forty-five kopecks now. At our place, no fear — anyone who comes can have all they can eat."
"The master's a tight one," added the counting-house clerk.
"Well, did you like their horses?" Dolly asked.

"The horses — no question about them. And the food was good. But it felt sort of dreary there to me, Darya Alexandrovna. I don't know what you thought," he said, turning his handsome, good-natured face to her.
"I thought the same. Well — shall we be home by evening?"
"We'd better be!"

Arriving home and finding everyone perfectly fine and especially charming, Darya Alexandrovna launched in with great animation, telling them about the trip out, how warmly she had been received, the luxury and good taste in which the Vronskys lived, their amusements — and she would not allow a word against them.

"You have to know Anna and Vronsky — I've got to know him better now — to see how lovely they are, and how touching," she said, speaking now with complete sincerity, forgetting the vague feeling of dissatisfaction and awkwardness she had felt while she was there.

title: Chapter 25
paragraphs: Vronsky and Anna spent the whole summer and part of the winter in the country, living in exactly the same situation and still taking no steps to obtain a divorce. They had an unspoken agreement not to go anywhere; but the longer they lived on their own — especially in the autumn, with no guests in the house — the more clearly both of them felt that they could not keep this up, and that something would have to change.

Their life looked as if nothing better could be wished for. They had abundance of everything; they had a child; and both had something to occupy them. Anna paid just as much attention to her appearance when there were no visitors, and she read a great deal — both novels and whatever serious literature was in fashion. She ordered every book praised in the foreign newspapers and reviews she received, and read them with that concentrated attention you only give to what you read in seclusion. On top of that, she studied in books and specialist journals every subject Vronsky took an interest in, so that he often went straight to her with questions about agriculture or architecture, sometimes even about horse-breeding or sport. He was amazed at her knowledge, her memory — at first he was inclined to doubt it, to ask her to back up her facts; and she would find what he wanted in some book and show him.

The hospital project interested her too. She didn't just help — she planned and proposed a great deal herself. But her main thought was still about herself: how dear was she to Vronsky? how far could she make up to him for everything he had given up? Vronsky appreciated this drive not just to please but to serve him, which had become the sole aim of her life; but at the same time he was wearied by the loving snares she used to hold him fast. As time passed and he found himself caught in those snares more and more often, he had a steadily growing desire — not so much to escape them as to test whether they hindered his freedom. If it hadn't been for this growing desire to be free, not to have a scene every time he wanted to go into town for a meeting or a race, Vronsky would have been perfectly satisfied with his life. The role he had taken up — that of a wealthy landowner, one of a class that ought to be the heart of the Russian aristocracy — was entirely to his taste; and now, after six months in that character, he found it even more satisfying. And his management of his estate, which absorbed and occupied him more and more, was a real success. In spite of the enormous sums spent on the hospital, on machinery, on cows ordered from Switzerland and many other things, he was convinced he wasn't squandering his fortune but increasing it. On anything to do with income — the sales of timber, wheat, and wool, the letting of land — Vronsky was hard as rock, and knew how to hold his prices. In all large-scale operations on this estate and his others, he stuck to the simplest methods that involved no risk, and on the small details he was careful and exacting to an extreme. In spite of all the cunning and ingenuity of the German steward — who would try to tempt him into purchases by making his original estimate always far larger than was really needed, and then suggesting to Vronsky that the thing might be had cheaper, turning a profit — Vronsky didn't budge. He listened to his steward, cross-examined him, and only agreed to his suggestions when the implement to be ordered or built was the very newest sort, not yet known in Russia and likely to cause a stir. Apart from such exceptions, he was willing to spend more only where there was a surplus, and when he did spend he went into the smallest details and insisted on getting the very best for the money — so that the way he handled his affairs made it clear that he wasn't wasting his fortune but building it up.
In October there were provincial elections in the Kashinsky province, where the estates of Vronsky, Sviazhsky, Koznishev, Oblonsky, and a small piece of Levin's land lay.

These elections were drawing public attention because of several things to do with them, and because of the people taking part. They had been much talked about, and great preparations were under way. People who never attended elections were coming from Moscow, from Petersburg, and from abroad to be there. Vronsky had promised Sviazhsky some time before that he'd go. In the run-up to the elections Sviazhsky, who often dropped in at Vozdvizhenskoe, drove over to fetch him. The day before, there had been very nearly a quarrel between Vronsky and Anna over this proposed trip. It was the bleakest sort of autumn weather, which is so dreary in the country, and so, bracing himself for a fight, Vronsky, with a hard, cold expression, told Anna he was leaving in a tone he had never used with her before. To his surprise, Anna took the news with complete composure and only asked when he'd be back. He looked at her closely, unable to account for this calm. She smiled at his look. He knew that way she had of withdrawing into herself, and he knew it only happened when she had decided on something without letting him in on her plans. He was afraid of it; but he was so anxious to avoid a scene that he kept up appearances, and half sincerely believed in what he longed to believe — her reasonableness.
"I hope you won't be too bored?"
"I hope not," Anna said. "I got a box of books from Gautier's yesterday. No, I won't be bored."
"She's trying to take that tone, and so much the better," he thought, "or else it would be the same thing all over again."

And he set off for the elections without pressing her for a frank explanation. It was the first time since the start of their intimacy that he had parted from her without one. From one angle that troubled him; from another he felt it was better this way. "At first there will be, as this time, something undefined held back, and then she'll get used to it. I can give up anything for her — but not my masculine independence," he thought.

title: Chapter 26
paragraphs: In September Levin moved to Moscow for Kitty's confinement. He had spent a whole month in Moscow with nothing to do, when Sergey Ivanovitch, who owned property in the Kashinsky province and was very interested in the coming elections, made ready to set off there. He invited his brother — who had a vote in the Seleznevsky district — to come along. Levin also had some extremely important business to handle in Kashin to do with the wardship of land, and the collection of certain redemption money for his sister, who was abroad.

Levin was still hesitating, but Kitty, seeing he was bored in Moscow and urging him to go, took it on herself to order him the proper nobleman's uniform, costing seven pounds. And that seven pounds spent on the uniform was the chief reason he finally decided to go. He went to Kashin.…

Levin had been in Kashin six days, visiting the assembly every day and busy with his sister's business, which still dragged on. The district marshals of nobility were all caught up in the elections, and it was impossible to get the simplest thing done that depended on the court of wardship. The other matter — the payment of the sums due — kept running into snags as well. After long negotiations over the legal details, the money was finally ready to be paid out; but the notary, a most obliging man, couldn't hand over the order, because it needed the president's signature, and the president, though he hadn't formally delegated his duties, was at the elections. All this wearisome wrangling — this endless going from place to place, talking with pleasant, excellent people who fully understood the unpleasantness of the petitioner's position but were powerless to help — all this effort that produced no result left Levin with a kind of misery, akin to the mortifying helplessness one feels in dreams when one tries to use physical force. He felt it again and again while talking to his most good-natured solicitor. The solicitor really did seem to be doing everything possible, going all out to get him out of his difficulties. "I'll tell you what to try," he said more than once; "go to so-and-so and so-and-so," and the solicitor drew up a proper plan for getting around the fatal sticking point that blocked everything. But he always added straightaway, "It'll mean some delay, of course, but you might try." And Levin did try, and did go. Everyone was kind and civil, but the obstacle being skirted seemed to surface again in the end, and once more bar his way. The particularly maddening thing was that Levin couldn't make out who exactly he was up against, whose interest it was that his business should not be done. Nobody seemed to know; the solicitor certainly didn't. If Levin could have understood the reason, the way he could see why you only approach the ticket window of a railway station in single file, it wouldn't have been so vexing and tiresome. But with the obstructions in his business, no one could tell him why they existed.

But Levin had changed a good deal since his marriage; he was patient, and if he couldn't see why everything was arranged this way, he told himself that he wasn't in a position to judge without knowing the whole picture, that it must probably be so, and he tried not to fret.

At the elections too — attending them and taking part — he tried not to judge or pick fights, but to grasp as fully as he could the question that was so earnestly and ardently absorbing honest and excellent men whom he respected. Since his marriage so many new and serious sides of life had opened up to Levin, things he had once dismissed as unimportant because of his frivolous attitude, that he now assumed there must be some serious significance in the question of the elections too, and he tried to find it.

Sergey Ivanovitch explained to him the meaning and purpose of the proposed revolution in the elections. The marshal of the province, in whose hands the law placed the control of so many important public functions — the guardianship of wards (the very department giving Levin so much trouble at the moment), the management of large sums subscribed by the nobility of the province, the high schools — female, male, and military — and popular education on the new model, and finally the district council — that marshal, Snetkov, was a nobleman of the old school. He had run through an immense fortune; he was good-hearted, honest in his own way, but utterly without any grasp of the needs of modern times. He always took, in every question, the side of the nobility; he was openly opposed to the spread of popular education; and he had managed to give a purely partisan character to the district council, which by rights ought to be of immense importance. What was needed was to put in his place a fresh, capable, completely modern man with contemporary ideas, and to frame their policy so as to draw, from the rights granted to the nobles — not as nobility, but as a constituent of the district council — every power of self-government those rights could possibly yield. In the wealthy Kashinsky province, which always led the others in everything, there was now such a balance of forces that this policy, once carried through there properly, might serve as a model for other provinces — for all Russia. And so the whole question was of the greatest importance. The plan was to elect as marshal, in Snetkov's place, either Sviazhsky or, better still, Nevyedovsky — a former university professor, a man of remarkable intelligence and a great friend of Sergey Ivanovitch.

The meeting was opened by the governor, who made a speech to the nobles, urging them to elect their public officials not out of favoritism but for the service and welfare of their fatherland, and expressing the hope that the honorable nobility of the Kashinsky province would, as at every previous election, hold their duty as sacred and justify the lofty confidence of the monarch.

When he finished his speech, the governor walked out of the hall, and the noblemen noisily and eagerly — some even enthusiastically — followed him and crowded around him as he put on his fur coat and chatted amicably with the marshal of the province. Levin, anxious not to miss anything, stood there too in the crowd, and heard the governor say, "Please tell Marya Ivanovna my wife is very sorry she couldn't come to the Home." After that the nobles, in fine spirits, sorted out their fur coats and all drove off to the cathedral.

In the cathedral Levin, raising his hand like everyone else and repeating the words of the archdeacon, swore the most terrible oaths to do everything the governor had hoped they would. Church services always moved Levin, and as he spoke the words "I kiss the cross" and glanced around at the crowd of young and old men echoing the same, he felt something stir in him.

On the second and third days there was business relating to the finances of the nobility and the girls' high school — of no importance whatsoever, as Sergey Ivanovitch explained — and Levin, busy with his own affairs, didn't attend the meetings. On the fourth day there was an audit of the marshal's accounts at the high table of the marshal of the province. And then came the first skirmish between the new party and the old. The committee deputed to verify the accounts reported to the meeting that everything was in order. The marshal of the province rose, thanked the nobility for their trust, and shed tears. The nobles gave him a loud ovation and shook his hand. But at that moment a nobleman of Sergey Ivanovitch's party said he had heard the committee had not actually verified the accounts, considering such a check an insult to the marshal of the province. One member of the committee carelessly admitted this. Then a small gentleman, very young-looking but very malicious, started saying it would probably be agreeable to the marshal of the province to give an account of his expenditures of public moneys, and that the misplaced delicacy of the committee was depriving him of that moral satisfaction. Then the committee members tried to retract their admission, and Sergey Ivanovitch began to argue that they had to logically admit either that they had verified the accounts or that they hadn't, and he laid out the dilemma in detail. Sergey Ivanovitch was answered by the spokesman of the opposing party. Then Sviazhsky spoke, and then the malicious gentleman again. The discussion lasted a long time and ended in nothing. Levin was surprised they could argue over the matter for so long, especially when, on asking Sergey Ivanovitch whether he supposed money had been misappropriated, Sergey Ivanovitch answered:
"Oh, no! He's an honest man. But those old-fashioned paternal-family methods of running provincial affairs have to be broken down."

On the fifth day the elections of the district marshals took place. It was a fairly stormy day in several districts. In the Seleznevsky district Sviazhsky was elected unanimously, without a ballot, and he gave a dinner that evening.

title: Chapter 27
paragraphs: The sixth day was fixed for the election of the marshal of the province.

The rooms, large and small, were packed with noblemen in every kind of uniform. Many had come just for that day. Men who hadn't seen each other in years — some from the Crimea, some from Petersburg, some from abroad — met in the rooms of the Hall of Nobility. There was a great deal of discussion around the governor's table under the portrait of the Tsar.

The nobles, in both the larger and the smaller rooms, grouped themselves in camps, and from their hostile, suspicious looks, from the silence that fell when outsiders approached a group, and from the way some of them drew off to whisper in the far corridor, it was clear that each side had its own secrets. In appearance the noblemen split sharply into two classes: the old and the new. The old wore for the most part the old-style uniforms of the nobility, buttoned all the way up, with spurs and hats — or else their own naval, cavalry, infantry, or official uniforms. The uniforms of the older men were embroidered in the old fashion, with epaulets on their shoulders; they were unmistakably tight and short in the waist, as if their wearers had outgrown them. The younger men wore the nobility uniform with long waists and broad shoulders, unbuttoned over white waistcoats, or uniforms with black collars and the embroidered insignia of justices of the peace. The court uniforms that brightened up the crowd here and there belonged to the younger set.

But the division between young and old didn't match the division between the parties. Some of the young men, Levin noticed, belonged to the old party; and some of the very oldest noblemen, on the other hand, were whispering with Sviazhsky and were clearly ardent partisans of the new party.

Levin stood in the smaller room, where they were smoking and having light refreshments, close to his own circle, and listening to what they were saying he conscientiously applied his whole mind to working out what was meant. Sergey Ivanovitch was the center around which the others gathered. At that moment he was listening to Sviazhsky and Hliustov, the marshal of another district, who belonged to their party. Hliustov refused to go with his district to ask Snetkov to stand, while Sviazhsky was trying to persuade him to do so, and Sergey Ivanovitch approved the plan. Levin couldn't work out why the opposition would ask the marshal to stand when they wanted to replace him.
Stepan Arkadyevitch, who had just finished a drink and a bite of lunch, came up to them in his uniform of a gentleman of the bedchamber, wiping his lips with a perfumed, hemmed batiste handkerchief.
"We are deploying our forces," he said, tugging at his whiskers. "Sergey Ivanovitch!"
And after listening to the conversation, he came down on Sviazhsky's side.
"One district is enough, and Sviazhsky is obviously in opposition," he said — words evidently clear to everyone but Levin.

"Why, Kostya, you here too! Don't tell me you've been converted, eh?" he added, turning to Levin and slipping his arm through his. Levin would gladly have been converted, but he couldn't make out the point at issue, and stepping a few paces away from the others, he explained to Stepan Arkadyevitch his inability to see why the marshal of the province had to be asked to stand.

_"O sancta simplicitas!"_ said Stepan Arkadyevitch, and briefly, clearly, he explained it. If, as in previous elections, every district asked the marshal of the province to stand, he would be elected without a ballot. That mustn't happen. Now eight districts had agreed to call on him: if two refused, Snetkov might decline to stand at all, and then the old party could pick another of their own, which would throw the whole calculation off. But if only one district — Sviazhsky's — did not call on him, Snetkov would let himself go to a ballot. Some of them were even going to vote for him on purpose, and let him pick up a good many votes, so the enemy would be thrown off the scent, and when a candidate from the other side was put up, they could give him some votes too. Levin understood up to a point, but not entirely, and was about to ask a few more questions when suddenly everyone started talking at once and making a racket, and they moved into the big room.

"What is it? Eh? Who?" "No guarantee? Whose? What?" "They won't pass him?" "No guarantee?" "They won't let Flerov in?" "Because of the charge against him?" "At this rate they won't admit anyone. It's a swindle!" "The law!" Levin heard exclamations from every side, and he moved into the big room with everyone else, all of them hurrying somewhere, afraid of missing something. Squeezed by the crowding noblemen, he made his way to the high table where the marshal of the province, Sviazhsky, and the other leaders were hotly debating something.

title: Chapter 28
paragraphs: Levin was standing some distance away. A nobleman beside him, breathing heavily and hoarsely, and another whose thick boots were creaking, kept him from hearing clearly. He could only faintly catch the marshal's soft voice, then the shrill voice of the malicious gentleman, and then Sviazhsky's voice. They were arguing, as far as he could make out, over the interpretation of the act and the exact meaning of the words: "liable to be called up for trial."

The crowd parted to let Sergey Ivanovitch through to the table. Sergey Ivanovitch waited until the malicious gentleman had finished, then said that he thought the best solution would be to refer to the act itself, and asked the secretary to find it. The act said that in case of disagreement, there had to be a ballot.

Sergey Ivanovitch read out the act and began to explain its meaning, but at that point a tall, stout, round-shouldered landowner with dyed whiskers, in a tight uniform that bit into the back of his neck, cut him off. He stepped up to the table and, striking it with his finger ring, shouted at the top of his voice: "A ballot! Put it to the vote! No need for more talking!" Then several voices broke out all at once, and the tall nobleman with the ring, more and more worked up, shouted louder and louder. But you couldn't make out what he was saying.

He was shouting for the very course Sergey Ivanovitch had proposed; but it was obvious that he hated him and his whole party, and this hatred ran through that whole party, and stirred up in opposition the same vindictiveness — though in a more decorous form — on the other side. Shouts went up, and for a moment everything was in confusion, so that the marshal of the province had to call for order.

"A ballot! A ballot! Every nobleman sees it! We shed our blood for our country!… The confidence of the monarch.… No checking the marshal's accounts; he's not a cashier.… But that's not the point.… Votes, please! Disgraceful!…" furious, violent voices shouted on all sides. The looks and faces were even more violent and furious than the words. They expressed the most implacable hatred. Levin had no idea what it was all about, and he marveled at the passion with which they were arguing whether or not the decision about Flerov should be put to a vote. He forgot — as Sergey Ivanovitch explained to him later — this syllogism: that it was necessary for the public good to get rid of the marshal of the province; that to get rid of the marshal a majority of votes was needed; that to get that majority Flerov's right to vote had to be secured; that to secure recognition of Flerov's right to vote, the interpretation of the act had to be settled.

"And one vote may decide the whole question, and one has to be serious and consistent, if one means to be of use in public life," Sergey Ivanovitch concluded. But Levin had forgotten all that, and it pained him to see all these excellent people, for whom he had respect, in such an unpleasant, vicious state of agitation. To escape that painful feeling, he slipped off into the other room where there was no one except the waiters at the refreshment bar. Watching the waiters busy with washing the crockery and setting out the plates and wine-glasses, seeing their calm and cheerful faces, Levin felt an unexpected sense of relief, as if he'd come out of a stuffy room into fresh air. He began to walk up and down, pleased to look at the waiters. He particularly liked the way one gray-whiskered waiter, who openly looked down on the younger ones and was teased by them in return, was teaching them how to fold napkins properly. Levin was about to strike up a conversation with the old waiter when the secretary of the court of wardship — a little old man whose specialty was knowing every nobleman in the province by name and patronymic — drew him away.
"Please come, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," he said. "Your brother's looking for you. They're voting on the legal point."

Levin walked into the room, was handed a white ball, and followed his brother, Sergey Ivanovitch, to the table where Sviazhsky was standing with a significant, ironical expression, holding his beard in his fist and sniffing at it. Sergey Ivanovitch slid his hand into the box, put the ball somewhere, and, making room for Levin, stopped. Levin stepped up, but having completely forgotten what he was supposed to do, and rather flustered, he turned to Sergey Ivanovitch with the question, "Where do I put it?" He asked softly, at a moment when there was conversation going on nearby, hoping his question wouldn't be overheard. But the people speaking paused, and his improper question was heard. Sergey Ivanovitch frowned.
"That's a matter for each man to decide," he said sternly.

Several people smiled. Levin flushed crimson, hurriedly thrust his hand under the cloth, and put the ball on the right, since it was in his right hand. Once he had, he remembered he should have put his left hand in too, and so he stuck it in — too late — and, more flustered than ever, retreated to the back.

"A hundred and twenty-six for admission! Ninety-eight against!" sang out the voice of the secretary, who couldn't pronounce the letter _r_. Then there was laughter; a button and two nuts were found in the box. The nobleman was granted the right to vote, and the new party had won.

But the old party did not consider themselves beaten. Levin heard them asking Snetkov to stand, and he saw a crowd of noblemen surrounding the marshal, who was saying something. Levin moved closer. In reply Snetkov spoke of the trust the noblemen of the province had placed in him, of the affection they had shown — which he didn't deserve, his only merit being his devotion to the nobility, to whom he had given twelve years of service. Several times he repeated, "I have served to the best of my ability, with truth and good faith — I value your kindness and I thank you," and suddenly he broke off, choking on tears, and walked out of the room. Whether those tears came from a sense of the injustice being done him, or from his love for the nobility, or from the strain of his situation, feeling himself surrounded by enemies, his emotion caught the assembly; most were touched, and Levin felt a tenderness for Snetkov.
In the doorway the marshal of the province bumped into Levin.

"Beg pardon, excuse me, please," he said, as if to a stranger; then, recognizing Levin, he smiled shyly. It seemed to Levin he would have liked to say something but couldn't, for emotion. His face and his whole figure in his uniform with its crosses, and the white trousers striped with braid, as he hurried along, reminded Levin of some hunted animal that sees it's done for. This expression in the marshal's face especially moved Levin, because only the day before he had been at his house on his trustee business and had seen him in all his grandeur — a kind-hearted, fatherly man. The big house with its old family furniture; the rather dirty, far-from-stylish but respectful footmen, plainly old house serfs who had stayed loyal to their master; the stout, good-natured wife in a lace cap and Turkish shawl, fussing over her pretty grandchild, her daughter's daughter; the young son, a sixth-form high school boy, coming home from school and greeting his father, kissing his big hand; the genuine, warm words and gestures of the old man — all of it had stirred in Levin the day before an instinctive feeling of respect and sympathy. This old man was a touching, pathetic figure to Levin now, and he longed to say something kind to him.
"So you're sure to be our marshal again," he said.
"That's not likely," said the marshal, looking around with a scared expression. "I'm worn out, I'm old. If there are men younger and worthier than I am, let them serve."
And the marshal disappeared through a side door.
The most solemn moment was at hand. They were going straight on to the election. The leaders of both parties were counting white and black on their fingers.

The argument over Flerov had given the new party not only Flerov's vote, but also extra time, so they could send for three noblemen who had been put out of action by the other party's maneuvers.
