Two noble gentlemen with a weakness for strong drink had been gotten drunk by Snetkov's partisans, and a third had had his uniform stolen.

Hearing about it, the new party had moved fast, during the dispute over Flerov, to send some of their men in a sledge to dress the stripped gentleman and to bring along one of the drunk ones to the meeting.
"I've brought one — doused him with water," said the landowner who had gone on this errand to Sviazhsky. "He'll do. He's all right."
"Not too drunk? He won't fall down?" said Sviazhsky, shaking his head.
"No, he's first-rate. As long as they don't give him any more here.… I've told the waiter not to serve him a drop, no matter what."

title: Chapter 29
paragraphs: The narrow room where they were smoking and having refreshments was packed with noblemen. The excitement was steadily rising, and every face showed some uneasiness. It was especially sharp in the leaders of each party, who knew every detail and had counted every vote. They were the generals organizing the coming battle. The rest, like the rank and file before an engagement, were getting themselves ready for the fight but looking in the meantime for other distractions. Some were eating, standing at the bar or sitting at tables; others were walking up and down the long room, smoking cigarettes, and talking with friends they hadn't seen in a long time.

Levin had no appetite, and he wasn't smoking; he didn't want to join his own circle — that is, Sergey Ivanovitch, Stepan Arkadyevitch, Sviazhsky and the rest — because Vronsky, in his equerry's uniform, was standing with them in eager conversation. Levin had already seen him at the meeting the day before, and had deliberately avoided him, not wanting to greet him. He went over to the window and sat down, scanning the groups and listening to what was being said around him. He felt low — especially because everyone else, as he saw, was eager, anxious, and engaged, while he alone, beside an old, toothless little man with mumbling lips wearing a naval uniform, had no part in any of it and nothing to do.

"He's such a blackguard! I've told him as much, and it makes no difference. Just think — he couldn't collect it in three years!" he heard, said with vigor by a round-shouldered, short country gentleman, his pomaded hair lying on his embroidered collar, his new boots — obviously put on for the occasion — heels tapping energetically as he spoke. Casting a displeased glance at Levin, this gentleman sharply turned his back.
"Yes, it's a dirty business, no question," a small gentleman agreed in a high voice.
Next, a whole crowd of country gentlemen surrounding a stout general came hurrying near Levin. These men were clearly looking for a place where they could talk without being overheard.
"How dare he say I had his breeches stolen! Pawned them for drink, more likely. Damn the man — prince indeed! He'd better not say it, the beast!"
"But excuse me! They're standing on the act," was being said in another group; "the wife has to be registered as noble."
"Oh, damn your acts! I speak from my heart. We're all gentlemen, aren't we? Above suspicion."
"Shall we go on, your excellency, _fine champagne?_"
Another group was trailing after a nobleman shouting something at the top of his voice — one of the three intoxicated gentlemen.

"I always told Marya Semyonovna to let it out for a fair rent, she'll never turn a profit otherwise," he heard a pleasant voice say. The speaker was a country gentleman with gray whiskers, in the regimental uniform of an old general staff officer. It was the very landowner Levin had met at Sviazhsky's. He recognized him at once. The landowner stared back at Levin, and they exchanged greetings.
"Very glad to see you! Of course! I remember you very well. Last year at our district marshal's, Nikolay Ivanovitch's."
"Well, how's the land treating you?" Levin asked.

"Oh, same as ever — always at a loss," the landowner answered with a resigned smile, but with an air of serenity and conviction that it could be no other way. "And what brings you to our province?" he asked. "Come to take part in our _coup d'état?_" he added, confidently pronouncing the French phrase with a bad accent. "All Russia's here — gentlemen of the bedchamber, everything just short of the ministry." He pointed to the imposing figure of Stepan Arkadyevitch in his white trousers and court uniform, walking past with a general.
"I have to admit I don't really understand what the provincial elections are about," Levin said.
The landowner looked at him.

"Why, what's there to understand? There's no meaning in it at all. It's a decaying institution, kept going only by sheer inertia. Just look — the very uniforms tell you it's an assembly of justices of the peace, permanent members of the court, and so on — not of noblemen."
"Then why do you come?" Levin asked.

"Habit, nothing more. And then one has to keep up connections. It's a kind of moral obligation. And, to tell the truth, there are one's own interests too. My son-in-law wants to stand as a permanent member; they're not rich people, and he has to be brought forward. These gentlemen, now, what are they here for?" he said, pointing at the malicious gentleman, who was talking at the high table.
"That's the new generation of nobility."
"New it may be, but nobility it isn't. They're some sort of proprietors, but we're the landowners. As noblemen, they're cutting their own throats."
"But you say it's an institution that's had its day."

"That may be, but still it ought to be treated with a little more respect. Snetkov, now.… We may be useful, or we may not, but we're the growth of a thousand years. If we're laying out a garden, planning one out in front of the house — and there's a tree standing on the very spot, one that's been there for centuries.… Old and gnarled it may be, but you don't cut the old fellow down to make room for the flower beds — you lay your beds out so as to make use of the tree. You won't grow him back in a year," he said carefully, and at once changed the subject. "Well, and how's your land doing?"
"Oh, not very well. I make five percent."

"Yes, but you're not counting your own labor. Aren't you worth something too? Take my own case. Before I took the land in hand I had a salary of three hundred pounds from the service. Now I work harder than I did in the service, and like you I get five percent on the land, and I thank God for it. But my own labor goes in for nothing."
"Then why do you do it, if it's a straight loss?"

"Oh, well, one does it! What would you have? It's habit, and one knows it's how it should be. And what's more," the landowner went on, leaning his elbows on the windowsill and chatting away, "my son, I have to tell you, has no taste for it. No doubt he'll be a man of science. So there'll be no one to keep it up. And still one does it. This year I've planted an orchard."
"Yes, yes," said Levin. "That's perfectly true. I always feel there's no real net gain in my work on the land, and yet one does it.… It's a kind of duty one feels toward the land."

"But I'll tell you what," the landowner went on. "A neighbor of mine, a merchant, came to my place. We walked around the fields and the garden. 'No,' he says, 'Stepan Vassilievitch — everything's well looked after, but your garden's neglected.' Whereas, in fact, it's kept up well. 'To my mind, I'd cut down that lime tree. Here you've got thousands of limes, and each one would make two good bundles of bark. And these days that bark's worth something. I'd cut the lot down.'"

"And with what he made he'd buy more stock, or pick up some land for a song and let it out in parcels to the peasants," Levin added with a smile. He had clearly met those commercial calculations more than once. "And he'd make his fortune. But you and I have to thank God if we keep what we've got and leave it to our children."
"You're married, I hear?" said the landowner.
"Yes," Levin answered with proud satisfaction. "Yes, it's rather strange," he went on. "So we live without making anything, as though we were ancient vestals set to tend a fire."
The landowner chuckled into his white mustaches.

"There are some of us, too — like our friend Nikolay Ivanovitch, or Count Vronsky, who has settled here lately — who try to run their land as though it were a factory; but so far it leads to nothing but burning through capital."
"But why is it we don't do as the merchants do? Why don't we cut down our parks for timber?" Levin asked, returning to a thought that had struck him.

"Why — as you said, to keep the fire in. Besides, that isn't a nobleman's work. And our work as noblemen isn't done here at the elections, but yonder, each in his own corner. There's a class instinct, too, for what one ought and oughtn't to do. The peasants, now — I marvel at them sometimes; any decent peasant tries to take all the land he can. However bad the land, he'll work it. With no return, either. At a plain loss."
"Just like us," said Levin. "Very, very glad to have met you," he added, seeing Sviazhsky approach.
"And here we've met for the first time since we met at your place," the landowner said to Sviazhsky, "and we've had a good talk too."
"Well — have you been attacking the new order of things?" Sviazhsky said with a smile.
"That we're bound to do."
"Got it off your chest?"

title: Chapter 30
paragraphs: Sviazhsky took Levin's arm and led him over to his own friends.
This time there was no avoiding Vronsky. He was standing with Stepan Arkadyevitch and Sergey Ivanovitch, looking straight at Levin as he came near.
"Delighted! I believe I've had the pleasure of meeting you… at Princess Shtcherbatskaya's," he said, offering Levin his hand.
"Yes, I remember our meeting very well," Levin said, and going crimson, he turned away at once and started talking to his brother.

With a slight smile Vronsky went on talking with Sviazhsky, plainly without the slightest interest in striking up a conversation with Levin. But Levin, even as he talked with his brother, kept glancing back at Vronsky, trying to think of something to say to him to smooth over his rudeness.
"What are we waiting for now?" Levin asked, looking at Sviazhsky and Vronsky.
"For Snetkov. He has to refuse or agree to stand," Sviazhsky answered.
"Well, what's he done — agreed or not?"
"That's the point — he's done neither," said Vronsky.
"And if he refuses, who will stand?" Levin asked, looking at Vronsky.
"Whoever chooses to," said Sviazhsky.
"Will you?" Levin asked.
"Certainly not I," Sviazhsky said, looking flustered, and casting an alarmed glance at the malicious gentleman, who was standing next to Sergey Ivanovitch.
"Who, then? Nevyedovsky?" Levin said, feeling he was putting his foot in it.
But that was worse still. Nevyedovsky and Sviazhsky were the two candidates.
"I certainly won't, under any circumstances," answered the malicious gentleman.
This was Nevyedovsky himself. Sviazhsky introduced him to Levin.
"Well — finding it exciting too?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, winking at Vronsky. "It's something like a race. One could lay bets on it."
"Yes, it is keenly exciting," said Vronsky. "And once you take a thing up, you want to see it through. It's a fight!" he said, scowling and setting his powerful jaws.
"What a capable fellow Sviazhsky is! Sees it all so clearly."
"Oh, yes!" Vronsky agreed indifferently.

A silence fell, during which Vronsky — having to look at something — looked at Levin: at his feet, at his uniform, then at his face, and noticing the gloomy eyes fixed on him, he said something for the sake of saying it:
"How is it that you, living in the country all the time, aren't a justice of the peace? You're not in their uniform."

"Because I consider the justice of the peace a silly institution," Levin answered gloomily. He had been all this time looking for an opening with Vronsky, to smooth over his rudeness at their first meeting.
"I don't think so — quite the opposite," Vronsky said, with quiet surprise.

"It's a toy," Levin cut him off. "We don't need justices of the peace. In eight years I've never had a single thing to do with them. And whatever I did have, they decided wrongly. The justice of the peace is over thirty miles from me. For some matter of two roubles I'd have to send a lawyer who'd cost me fifteen."

And he went on to tell how a peasant had stolen some flour from the miller, and when the miller called him out on it, the peasant had lodged a complaint for slander. All of it was completely unnecessary and stupid, and Levin felt it himself even as he was saying it.
"Oh, what an original fellow!" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, with his most soothing, almond-oil smile. "But come along — I think they're voting…."
And they split up.

"I can't understand," said Sergey Ivanovitch, who had watched his brother's clumsiness, "I can't understand how anyone can be so completely without political tact. That's where we Russians fall short. The marshal of the province is our opponent, and you're _ami cochon_ with him, and you beg him to stand. Count Vronsky, now… I'm not making a friend of him; he's invited me to dinner and I won't go; but he's on our side — why turn him into an enemy? Then you ask Nevyedovsky whether he's going to stand. That's not done."
"Oh, I don't understand any of it! And it's all such nonsense," Levin answered gloomily.
"You say it's all such nonsense, but the moment you have anything to do with it, you make a muddle of it."
Levin didn't answer, and they walked together into the big room.

The marshal of the province, though he was vaguely aware of some trap being set for him, and though he hadn't been called upon by everyone to stand, had still made up his mind to do so. Silence fell across the room. The secretary announced in a loud voice that the captain of the guards, Mihail Stepanovitch Snetkov, would now be balloted for as marshal of the province.
The district marshals walked from their tables to the high table carrying plates with balls on them, and the election began.

"Put it on the right side," Stepan Arkadyevitch whispered, as he and his brother fell in behind their district marshal at the table. But Levin had by now forgotten the calculations that had been explained to him, and was afraid Stepan Arkadyevitch might be mistaken in saying "the right side." Surely Snetkov was the enemy. As he stepped up, he held the ball in his right hand, but, thinking he had it wrong, just at the box he switched it to his left hand, and unmistakably put the ball on the left. An expert in the business, standing at the box and able to tell from the mere motion of the elbow where each man put his ball, scowled with annoyance. His sharp eye was no use to him here.

Everything was quiet, and the counting of the balls could be heard. Then a single voice rose and announced the numbers for and against. The marshal had been voted in by a comfortable majority. There was an uproar and a rush toward the doors. Snetkov came in, and the noblemen thronged around him with their congratulations.
"Well, is it over now?" Levin asked Sergey Ivanovitch.
"It's only just beginning," Sviazhsky said with a smile, answering for Sergey Ivanovitch. "Some other candidate may receive more votes than the marshal."

Levin had completely forgotten about that. He could only remember now that there was some sort of maneuver involved, but he was too bored to think what it was. He felt low, and longed to get out of the crowd.

Since no one was paying him any attention and no one apparently needed him, he quietly slipped away into the little room where the refreshments were, and again felt a great sense of comfort at the sight of the waiters. The little old waiter pressed something on him, and Levin accepted. After eating a cutlet with beans and chatting with the waiters about their former masters, Levin, not wanting to go back to the hall where everything was so distasteful to him, set off to walk through the galleries. The galleries were full of fashionably dressed ladies, leaning over the balustrade, trying not to miss a single word of what was being said below. Sitting and standing with the ladies were smart lawyers, high school teachers in spectacles, and officers. Everywhere they were talking about the election — how worried the marshal had been, how splendid the speeches had been. In one group Levin heard his brother being praised. One lady was telling a lawyer:

"How glad I am I heard Koznishev! It was worth missing dinner for. He's exquisite! So clear and precise, all of it! There isn't one of you in the law courts who speaks like that. The only one is Meidel, and he's not nearly as eloquent."
Finding a free spot, Levin leaned over the balustrade and began to look and listen.
All the noblemen were sitting penned off behind barriers by district. In the middle of the room stood a man in a uniform, who shouted in a loud, high voice:
"As a candidate for the marshalship of the nobility of the province we call upon staff-captain Yevgeney Ivanovitch Apuhtin!" A dead silence followed, and then a weak old voice was heard: "Declined!"
"We call upon the privy councilor Pyotr Petrovitch Bol," the voice began again.
"Declined!" a high boyish voice answered.

Again it started, and again "Declined." And it went on like this for about an hour. Levin, elbows on the balustrade, watched and listened. At first he wondered and wanted to know what it meant; then, certain he couldn't make it out, he started to get bored. Then, recalling all the excitement and vindictiveness he had seen in every face, he felt sad; he decided to leave, and went downstairs. As he was passing through the entry to the galleries he met a dejected high school boy walking up and down with tired-looking eyes. On the stairs he met a couple — a lady running quickly on her high heels and the jaunty deputy prosecutor.
"I told you you weren't late," the deputy prosecutor was saying just as Levin stepped aside to let the lady go past.
Levin was on his way down to the exit and was just feeling in his waistcoat pocket for his overcoat number when the secretary caught up with him.
"This way, please, Konstantin Dmitrievitch — they're voting."

The candidate now being voted on was Nevyedovsky, who had so flatly denied any thought of standing. Levin went up to the door of the room; it was locked. The secretary knocked, the door opened, and Levin was met by two red-faced gentlemen who darted out.
"I can't take any more of it," said one of them.
After them the face of the marshal of the province poked out. His face looked dreadful — drained with exhaustion and dismay.
"I told you not to let anyone out!" he shouted at the doorkeeper.
"I let someone in, your excellency!"
"Mercy on us!" — and with a heavy sigh the marshal of the province walked to the high table in the middle of the room, head down, his legs unsteady in his white trousers.

Nevyedovsky had taken a higher majority, just as they had planned, and he was the new marshal of the province. Many were amused, many were pleased and happy, many were in ecstasies, many were disgusted and unhappy. The former marshal of the province was in a despair he couldn't hide. When Nevyedovsky left the room, the crowd thronged around him and followed him with the same enthusiasm with which they had followed the governor who opened the meetings, and Snetkov when he was elected.

title: Chapter 31
paragraphs: The newly elected marshal and many of the winning party dined that day at Vronsky's.

Vronsky had come to the elections partly because he was bored in the country and wanted to show Anna his right to independence, and also to repay Sviazhsky for the trouble he had taken on his behalf at the district council election by supporting him here — but chiefly in order to discharge to the letter all those duties of a nobleman and landowner he had taken on. He hadn't expected in the least that the election would so interest him, would excite him so keenly, or that he would be so good at this kind of thing. He was a complete newcomer to the circle of provincial nobility, but his success was unmistakable, and he wasn't wrong in supposing he had already gained a certain influence. This influence was due to his wealth and his reputation, the capital town house lent to him by his old friend Shirkov — who held a post in the department of finances and was director of a flourishing bank in Kashin; the excellent cook Vronsky had brought from the country; and his friendship with the governor, an old schoolfellow of his — and one he had patronized and protected, at that. But more than anything, what contributed to his success was his direct, even-tempered manner with everyone, which quickly made most of the noblemen reverse the current opinion that he was haughty. He was conscious himself that — apart from that whimsical gentleman married to Kitty Shtcherbatskaya, who had _à propos de bottes_ poured out a flood of irrelevant absurdities with such venomous fury — every nobleman he had gotten to know had come over to his side. He saw clearly, and other people saw it too, that he had done a great deal to secure Nevyedovsky's success. And now, at his own table, celebrating Nevyedovsky's election, he felt an agreeable sense of triumph over the success of his candidate. The election itself had so fascinated him that, if he could manage to be married within the next three years, he was beginning to think of standing himself — much as after winning a race ridden by a jockey, he had wanted to ride a race himself.

Today he was celebrating his jockey's success. Vronsky sat at the head of the table; on his right hand sat the young governor, a general of high rank. To everyone else he was the chief man in the province, who had solemnly opened the elections with his speech and had inspired respect and even awe in many — as Vronsky could see; to Vronsky he was little Katka Maslov — that had been his nickname in the Pages' Corps — and Vronsky could tell he was shy and tried to _mettre à son aise_. On the left sat Nevyedovsky with his youthful, stubborn, malicious face. With him Vronsky was straightforward and respectful.

Sviazhsky took his defeat very lightly. As he said himself, raising his glass to Nevyedovsky, it wasn't a defeat at all in his eyes; they couldn't have found a better representative of the new direction the nobility ought to follow. And so every honest person, he said, was on the side of today's success and was rejoicing over it.

Stepan Arkadyevitch was glad too — glad he was having a good time, and that everyone was pleased. The election affair made an excellent occasion for a first-rate dinner. Sviazhsky comically imitated the marshal's tearful speech, and observed, addressing Nevyedovsky, that his excellency would have to come up with some other, more complicated method of auditing the accounts than tears. Another nobleman jokingly described how footmen in stockings had been ordered for the marshal's ball, and how now they would have to be sent back unless the new marshal would give a ball with footmen in stockings.
Throughout dinner they kept calling Nevyedovsky "our marshal" and "your excellency."

It was said with the same pleasure with which a bride is called "Madame" and her husband's name. Nevyedovsky affected to be not merely indifferent to the title but scornful of it, though it was obvious he was delighted, and had to keep himself in check so as not to give away the kind of triumph that didn't fit the new liberal tone.

After dinner several telegrams were sent off to people interested in the outcome. And Stepan Arkadyevitch, in high good humor, sent Darya Alexandrovna a telegram: "Nevyedovsky elected by twenty votes. Congratulations. Pass it on." He dictated it aloud, saying, "We must let them share in our rejoicing." Darya Alexandrovna, when she got the message, simply sighed over the rouble wasted on it, and understood that it was an after-dinner affair. She knew Stiva had a weakness after dining for _faire jouer le télégraphe._

Everything — including the excellent dinner and the wine, not from Russian merchants but imported direct from abroad — was extremely dignified, simple, and enjoyable. The party — about twenty — had been picked by Sviazhsky from among the more active new liberals, all of the same way of thinking, who were at the same time clever and well bred. They drank, half jokingly, to the health of the new marshal of the province, of the governor, of the bank director, and of "our amiable host."
Vronsky was satisfied. He had never expected to find so pleasant a tone in the provinces.

Toward the end of dinner things were livelier still. The governor invited Vronsky to come to a concert for the benefit of the Servians, which his wife — eager to make his acquaintance — had been organizing.
"There'll be a ball, and you'll see the belle of the province. Worth seeing, really."
"Not in my line," Vronsky answered. He liked that English phrase. But he smiled, and promised to come.
Just before they got up from the table, while everyone was smoking, Vronsky's valet came up to him with a letter on a tray.
"From Vozdvizhenskoe by special messenger," he said with a significant expression.
"Astonishing — how like he is to the deputy prosecutor Sventitsky," one of the guests said in French of the valet, while Vronsky, frowning, read the letter.

The letter was from Anna. Before he read it, he knew what was in it. Expecting the elections to be over in five days, he had promised to be back on Friday. Today was Saturday, and he knew the letter contained reproaches for not being back at the time he had set. The letter he'd sent the evening before had probably not reached her yet.

The letter was what he had expected, but the form of it was unexpected, and particularly unpleasant to him. "Annie is very ill, the doctor says it may be inflammation. I am losing my head all alone. Princess Varvara is no help, only a hindrance. I expected you the day before yesterday, and yesterday, and now I am sending to find out where you are and what you are doing. I wanted to come myself, but thought better of it, knowing you would dislike it. Send some answer, so that I may know what to do."
The child ill — and yet she had thought of coming herself. Their daughter ill, and this hostile tone.
The innocent festivities over the election, and this gloomy, burdensome love he had to go back to, struck Vronsky by the contrast. But he had to go, and he set off home by the first train that night.

title: Chapter 32
paragraphs: Before Vronsky left for the elections, Anna had thought about the scenes they kept repeating every time he left the house, and how they might just push him away from her instead of binding him closer. She made up her mind to do everything she could to hold herself together and bear the parting calmly. But the cold, hard look he gave her when he came to tell her he was going wounded her, and her peace was already gone before he had even left.

Alone afterwards, turning over that look — the one that had told her plainly he had the right to do as he pleased — she ended up where she always did: at the feeling of her own humiliation. "He has the right to go away whenever and wherever he wants. Not only to go away — to leave me. He has every right and I have none. But knowing that, he ought not to do it. And what has he done, really?... He looked at me with a cold, severe expression. Of course it's something vague, intangible, but it was never like that before, and that look means a great deal," she thought. "That look is the beginning of indifference."

And although she was sure his coldness was setting in, there was nothing she could do about it; she could not change anything between them. As before, she could only hold him through love and through her charm. And as before, she could only smother the terrifying thought of what would happen if he stopped loving her — by keeping busy in the daytime and by morphine at night. There was still one other way; not to hold him — because for that she wanted nothing more than his love — but to be closer to him, so situated that he would not leave her. That way was divorce and marriage. She began to long for it, and resolved to agree the first time he or Stiva brought it up.
Taken up with these thoughts, she got through the five days he was at the elections without him.

Walks, conversation with Princess Varvara, visits to the hospital, and above all reading — one book after another — filled her time. But on the sixth day, when the coachman returned without him, she felt she could no longer hold back the thought of him and what he was doing there. Just then her little girl fell ill. Anna started looking after her, but even that did not distract her, especially since the illness was not serious. However hard she tried, she could not love this little child, and she had no power to pretend she did. Toward the evening of that day, still alone, Anna was in such a panic about him that she decided to set off for town; then she thought again and wrote him the contradictory letter Vronsky received, and without reading it through she sent it off with a special messenger. The next morning she got his letter and regretted her own. She dreaded a repeat of the harsh look he had thrown at her at parting, especially now that he knew the baby was not in any real danger. Still she was glad she had written. At this moment Anna was openly admitting to herself that she was a burden to him, that he would give up his freedom to return to her unwillingly, and yet she was glad he was coming. Let him grow tired of her — he would still be here with her, where she could see him and know what he did at every moment.

She was sitting in the drawing room near a lamp with a new volume of Taine, reading, listening to the wind outside, every minute expecting the carriage. Several times she thought she heard wheels and was wrong. At last she heard not the wheels but the coachman's shout and the muffled rumble in the covered entry. Even Princess Varvara, dealing out her game of patience, confirmed it, and Anna, blushing hot, stood up — but instead of going down, as she had twice before, she stayed where she was. She felt suddenly ashamed of her own double-dealing, but more than that she was afraid of how he might look at her. All the hurt pride was gone now; she was only afraid of seeing his displeasure. She remembered that for the last two days her child had been completely well again. She felt positively annoyed with the girl for getting better just at the moment her letter had gone off. Then she thought of him — that he was here, all of him, his hands, his eyes. She heard his voice. And forgetting everything, she ran joyfully out to meet him.
"Well, how is Annie?" he said timidly from below, looking up at her as she came running down to him.
He was sitting on a chair while a footman pulled off one of his warm overshoes.
"Oh, she's better."
"And you?" he said, shaking himself.
She took his hand in both of hers and drew it to her waist, not taking her eyes off him.

"Well, I'm glad," he said, coolly looking her over — her hair, her dress, which he knew she had put on for him. It was all charming, but how many times had it charmed him already! And the stern, stony expression she so dreaded settled on his face.
"Well, I'm glad. And are you well?" he said, wiping his damp beard with his handkerchief and kissing her hand.
"Never mind," she thought. "Only let him be here — and as long as he is, he cannot, he dare not, stop loving me."
The evening passed pleasantly and cheerfully with Princess Varvara, who complained to him that Anna had been taking morphine while he was away.
"What was I to do? I couldn't sleep.... My thoughts wouldn't leave me alone. When he's here I never take it — almost never."

He told her about the election, and Anna, with well-aimed questions, drew him to what pleased him most — his own success. She told him about everything at home that would interest him; and everything she told him was as cheerful as she could make it.
But late in the evening, when they were alone, Anna, feeling that she had fully won him back, wanted to wipe away the painful impression of the look he had given her over her letter. She said:
"Tell me honestly — you were annoyed at getting my letter, and you didn't believe me?"
The moment she said it she felt that however warmly he felt toward her now, he had not forgiven her for it.
"Yes," he said. "The letter was strange. First Annie ill, and then you thinking of coming yourself."
"It was all true."
"Oh, I don't doubt it."
"Yes, you do doubt it. You're annoyed, I can see."
"Not for a moment. I'm only annoyed, that's true, that you somehow don't want to admit that there are duties...."
"The duty of going to a concert...."
"But we won't talk about it," he said.
"Why not talk about it?" she said.

"I only meant to say that genuinely important things can come up. Now, for instance, I'll have to go to Moscow to settle things about the house.... Oh, Anna, why are you so irritable? Don't you know I can't live without you?"
"If that's so," said Anna, her voice changing all at once, "then it means you're sick of this life.... Yes, you'll come for a day and go away again, the way men do...."
"Anna, that's cruel. I'm ready to give up my whole life."
But she did not hear him.
"If you go to Moscow, I'll go too. I won't stay here. Either we separate or we live together."
"Look, you know that's the one thing I want. But for that to happen...."
"We have to get a divorce. I'll write to him. I see I can't go on like this.... But I'll come with you to Moscow."
"You talk as if you were threatening me. But there's nothing I want more than never to be parted from you," said Vronsky, smiling.
But as he said this, what gleamed in his eyes was not merely a cold look but the vindictive look of a man who has been hounded into cruelty.
She saw the look and read it correctly.
"If so, it's a disaster!" that glance told her. It was the impression of a moment, but she never forgot it.

Anna wrote to her husband asking for a divorce, and toward the end of November, taking leave of Princess Varvara — who wanted to go to Petersburg — she went with Vronsky to Moscow. Expecting an answer from Alexey Alexandrovitch any day, and after that the divorce, they settled in together now like a married couple.
PART SEVEN

title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: The Levins had been in Moscow three months. The date had long since passed on which, by the most trustworthy calculations of those who knew such things, Kitty should have given birth. But she was still up and about, and there was no sign that her time was any closer than it had been two months earlier. The doctor, the monthly nurse, Dolly and her mother, and Levin most of all — who could not think of what was coming without dread — began to grow impatient and uneasy. Kitty was the only one who felt perfectly calm and happy.

She was clearly aware now of a new feeling of love being born in her for the child to come — for someone who in a sense already existed — and she dwelt on this feeling in bliss. He was not entirely a part of herself any more; sometimes he lived his own life apart from her. Often this separate being gave her pain, and at the same time she wanted to laugh out of a strange new joy.

All the people she loved were with her, and they were all so good to her, took such tender care of her, and everything around her was made so pleasant, that if she had not known and felt it must all end soon, she could not have wished for a better, sweeter life. The one thing that spoiled the charm of it was that her husband was not what she liked him to be, the way he had been in the country.

She loved his calm, friendly, hospitable manner in the country. In town he seemed continually on edge and on guard, as if he were afraid someone would be rude to him — and even more rude to her. At home in the country, knowing exactly that he was in his proper place, he was never in a hurry to be off somewhere else. He was never idle. Here in town he was always rushing, as if he were afraid of missing something, and yet he had nothing to do. And she felt sorry for him. To others, she knew, he did not look like a man to pity. On the contrary, when Kitty watched him in company — the way one sometimes looks at the people one loves, trying to see him as if he were a stranger, to catch the impression he must make on others — she saw with a panic that was almost jealous fear that he was far from being a pitiable figure. He was very attractive: his fine breeding, his slightly old-fashioned, reserved courtesy with women, his strong build, and his striking, expressive face — all of it. But she saw him not from outside but from within. She saw that here he was not himself; that was the only way she could put his state to herself. Sometimes she silently reproached him for being unable to live in town; sometimes she had to admit that it really was hard for him to arrange his life here so that he could be content with it.

What was there for him to do, really? He didn't care for cards; he didn't go to a club. Spending his time with cheerful gentlemen of Oblonsky's sort — she knew now what that meant... it meant drinking, and then going somewhere after the drinking. She could not bear to think of where men went on those occasions. Was he to go into society? But she knew he could only enjoy that if he took pleasure in the company of young women, and she could hardly wish that. Was he to stay home with her, her mother, and her sisters? Much as she liked and enjoyed her sisters' endless conversation on the same old subjects — "Aline-Nadine," as the old prince called their talk — she knew it had to bore him. What was left for him to do? He had tried to go on with his book, and at first he used to go to the library, copying out passages and chasing down references. But, as he told her, the less he did, the less time he had to do anything in. And besides, he complained that he had talked about his book too much here, so that all his ideas about it were jumbled and had lost their interest for him.

One advantage of life in town was that quarrels hardly ever broke out between them here. Whether it was that the conditions were different, or that they had both become more careful and sensible about it, they had no quarrels in Moscow from jealousy, the very thing they had feared so much when they moved up from the country.
There was one event, an event of real importance to both of them from that point of view — Kitty's meeting with Vronsky.

Old Princess Marya Borissovna, Kitty's godmother, had always been very fond of her and insisted on seeing her. Kitty did not go into society at all because of her condition, but she went with her father to call on the venerable old lady, and there she ran into Vronsky.

The only thing Kitty could reproach herself for over this meeting was that the instant she recognized in his civilian clothes the features once so familiar to her, her breath caught, the blood rushed to her heart, and a bright blush — she felt it — spread across her face. But it only lasted a few seconds. Before her father, who deliberately started talking to Vronsky in a loud voice, had finished, she was perfectly ready to look at Vronsky, to speak to him if she had to, exactly as she spoke to Princess Marya Borissovna — and more than that, to do it in such a way that her husband, whose unseen presence she seemed to feel at her side, would have approved of every faint inflection and smile.

She said a few words to him, even smiled calmly at his joke about the elections, which he called "our parliament." (She had to smile to show she got the joke.) But she turned at once back to Princess Marya Borissovna and did not glance at him again until he stood up to leave; then she looked at him, but obviously only because it would have been rude not to look at a man saying good-bye.

She was grateful to her father for not saying anything to her about their meeting Vronsky, but she could tell from his special warmth toward her on their usual walk after the visit that he was pleased with her. She was pleased with herself. She had not expected to have the strength — while keeping every memory of her old feeling for Vronsky stored somewhere at the bottom of her heart — not just to seem but to actually be perfectly indifferent and composed with him.

Levin flushed far more than she did when she told him she had met Vronsky at Princess Marya Borissovna's. It was hard for her to tell him this, but harder still to go on giving him the details, since he did not ask any questions but only stared at her, frowning.

"I'm so sorry you weren't there," she said. "Not in the room — I couldn't have been as natural with you there ... I'm blushing much more now, much, much more," she said, blushing until tears came to her eyes. "But that you couldn't have watched through a crack."

Her truthful eyes told Levin that she was satisfied with herself, and despite her blushing he was quickly reassured and started questioning her, which was all she wanted. By the time he had heard everything, including the detail that for the first second she could not help blushing but afterwards was as direct and as much at ease as with any chance acquaintance, Levin was quite happy again and said he was glad, and would not behave as stupidly the next time as he had at the elections, but would try, the first time he met Vronsky, to be as friendly as he could.
"It's awful to feel that there's a man almost an enemy you find it painful to meet," said Levin. "I'm very, very glad."

title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: "Go, please — go and call on the Bols," Kitty said to her husband when he came in to see her at eleven before going out. "I know you're dining at the club; papa put your name down. But what are you going to do this morning?"
"I'm just going to Katavasov's," Levin answered.
"So early?"
"He promised to introduce me to Metrov. I wanted to talk to him about my work. He's a distinguished scientific man from Petersburg," said Levin.
"Yes — wasn't it his article you were praising? Well, and after that?" said Kitty.
"I'll probably go to the court, about my sister's case."
"And the concert?" she asked.
"I won't go there by myself."
"No? Do go; there are some new pieces.... You were so interested in them. I'd definitely go."
"Well, in any case I'll be home before dinner," he said, glancing at his watch.
"Put on your frock coat, so you can call on Countess Bola straight away."
"But is it really necessary?"
"Oh, absolutely! He's been to see us. Come on, what is it? You go in, sit down, talk for five minutes about the weather, get up, and leave."

"Oh, you wouldn't believe it! I've gotten so out of the habit of all this that it makes me feel positively ashamed. It's such a ridiculous thing to do! A complete outsider walks in, sits down, hangs around with nothing to do, wastes their time, makes himself miserable, and walks away!"
Kitty laughed.
"I suppose you used to pay calls before we were married, didn't you?"

"Yes, I did, but I always felt ashamed of it, and now I'm so out of the habit that, honestly, I'd sooner go two days running without dinner than make this call! You feel so foolish! The whole time I'm sure they're annoyed, that they're saying, 'What's he come for?'"
"No, they won't. I'll vouch for that," said Kitty, looking into his face with a laugh. She took his hand. "Well, good-bye.... Do go, please."
He was on the point of going out after kissing his wife's hand when she stopped him.
"Kostya, do you know I only have fifty roubles left?"
"Oh, all right, I'll go to the bank and get some. How much?" he said, with the look of dissatisfaction she knew so well.
"No, wait a minute." She held his hand. "Let's talk about it — it worries me. I don't think I spend on anything unnecessary, but money just seems to vanish. We're not managing well somehow."
"Oh, it's all right," he said, with a small cough, looking up at her from under his brows.

She knew that cough well. It was a sign of intense dissatisfaction — not with her, but with himself. He really was annoyed, not that so much money was being spent, but at being reminded of what he, sensing something was wrong, had wanted to forget.
"I've told Sokolov to sell the wheat and to take an advance on the mill. We'll have money enough in any case."
"Yes, but I'm afraid that, all together...."
"Oh, it's fine, fine," he repeated. "Well, good-bye, darling."
"No, I really am sorry sometimes that I listened to mamma. How lovely it would have been in the country! As it is, I'm worrying you all, and we're throwing money away."
"Not at all, not at all. Not once since I've been married have I said things could have been better than they are...."
"Truly?" she said, looking into his eyes.

He had said it without thinking, just to comfort her. But when he looked at her and saw those sweet, truthful eyes fixed on him questioningly, he repeated it from the heart. "I was actually forgetting her," he thought. And he remembered what was ahead of them, so soon to come.
"Will it be soon? How are you feeling?" he whispered, taking both her hands.
"I've thought so so many times that now I don't think about it or know anything about it."
"And you're not frightened?"
She smiled scornfully.
"Not the least little bit," she said.
"Well, if anything happens, I'll be at Katavasov's."

"No, nothing's going to happen, and don't think about it. I'm going for a walk on the boulevard with papa. We're going to see Dolly. I'll expect you before dinner. Oh, yes! Did you know that Dolly's situation has become completely impossible? She's in debt everywhere; she doesn't have a penny. Yesterday we were talking with mamma and Arseny" (this was her sister's husband Lvov), "and we've decided to send you with him to talk to Stiva. It really is unbearable. One can't speak to papa about it.... But if you and he...."
"What can we do, really?" said Levin.
"You'll be at Arseny's anyway; talk to him, he'll tell you what we decided."
"Oh, I agree in advance to whatever Arseny thinks. I'll go and see him. By the way, if I do go to the concert, I'll go with Natalia. Well, good-bye."
Out on the front steps Levin was stopped by Kouzma — the old servant who had been with him since before his marriage and now ran the household for them in town.
"Beauty" (that was the left shaft-horse they had brought up from the country) "has been badly shod and has gone quite lame," he said. "What does your honor want done?"

During the first part of their stay in Moscow, Levin had used his own horses brought up from the country. He had tried to arrange this side of their expenses as well and as cheaply as he could; but it turned out that their own horses cost more than hired ones, and they ended up hiring as well.
"Send for the vet — it may be a bruise."
"And for Katerina Alexandrovna?" Kouzma asked.

By now Levin was no longer struck, as he had been at first, by the fact that to get from one end of Moscow to the other he had to have two strong horses harnessed to a heavy carriage, drive three miles through the snowy slush, and keep the carriage standing there for four hours, paying five roubles every time.
Now it seemed entirely natural.
"Hire a pair for our carriage from the jobmaster," he said.
"Yes, sir."

And like that, simply and easily, thanks to the conveniences of town life, Levin settled a question that in the country would have called for a great deal of personal trouble and effort, and going out onto the steps he called a sledge, sat down, and drove to Nikitsky. On the way he thought no more about money but mused on the meeting ahead of him with the Petersburg savant, a writer on sociology, and what he would tell him about his book.

Only during the first days of his stay in Moscow had Levin been struck by the strange, unproductive but unavoidable spending that, to a man from the country, was expected of him on every side. Now he was used to it. The same thing had happened to him in this matter as is said to happen to drunkards — the first glass sticks in the throat, the second flies down like a hawk, and after the third they're like tiny little birds. When Levin changed his first hundred-rouble note to pay for liveries for his footmen and hall-porter, he could not help thinking that these liveries were of no use to anyone — but they were undeniably necessary, judging by the amazement on the faces of the princess and Kitty when he suggested they might do without them — that these liveries would cost the wages of two laborers for the summer, which is to say about three hundred working days from Easter to Ash Wednesday, each one a day of hard labor from early morning to late evening — and that hundred-rouble note did stick in his throat. But the next note, changed to pay for a dinner for their relatives that cost twenty-eight roubles — although it did make Levin reflect that twenty-eight roubles meant nine measures of oats, which men would have reaped and bound and threshed and winnowed and sifted and sown with groans and sweat — this next one he parted with more easily. And now the notes he changed no longer set off such reflections at all; they flew off like little birds. Whether the work that went into earning the money was worth the pleasure of what was bought with it — that was a question he had long since given up. His business calculation that there was a certain price below which he could not sell a particular grain was also forgotten. The rye, for the price of which he had held out so long, had been sold for fifty kopecks a measure cheaper than it had been fetching a month before. Even the awareness that at this rate of spending he could not last a year without debt no longer had any force. Only one thing was essential: to have money in the bank, without asking where it came from, so that he knew he had something to buy meat with tomorrow. And so far this condition had been met; there had always been money in the bank. But now the money in the bank was gone, and he had no clear idea where the next batch was coming from. This was what had bothered him at the moment Kitty mentioned money; but he had no time to think about it. He drove off, his mind on Katavasov and the meeting with Metrov that lay ahead.

title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: On this stay in town Levin had seen a great deal of his old university friend, Professor Katavasov, whom he had not seen since his marriage. He liked Katavasov for the clarity and simplicity of his view of life. Levin thought the clarity of Katavasov's view of life came from the poverty of his nature; Katavasov thought the loose ends in Levin's ideas came from a lack of intellectual discipline; but Levin enjoyed Katavasov's clarity, and Katavasov enjoyed the abundance of Levin's untrained ideas, and they liked to meet and argue.

Levin had read Katavasov some sections of his book, and Katavasov had liked them. The day before, Katavasov had run into Levin at a public lecture and told him that the famous Metrov, whose article Levin had so much admired, was in Moscow, was very interested in what Katavasov had told him about Levin's work, and was coming to see him tomorrow at eleven, and would be very glad to make Levin's acquaintance.

"You're a reformed character, I'm pleased to see," said Katavasov, meeting Levin in the little drawing room. "I heard the bell and thought: It can't be him, exactly on time!... Well, what do you say to the Montenegrins now? They're a race of warriors."
"Why — what's happened?" asked Levin.

Katavasov gave him the latest war news in a few words, and going into his study, he introduced Levin to a short, thickset man with a pleasant face. This was Metrov. The conversation touched briefly on politics and on how recent events were being seen in the higher circles in Petersburg. Metrov repeated a remark that had come to him from a most trustworthy source, said to have been uttered on the subject by the Tsar and one of his ministers. Katavasov had heard, on equally good authority, that the Tsar had said something quite different. Levin tried to imagine circumstances in which both remarks could have been made, and the conversation on that topic dropped.

"Yes — he has almost written a book on the natural conditions of the laborer in relation to the land," Katavasov said. "I'm not a specialist, but I, as a natural scientist, was pleased that he doesn't take mankind as something standing outside biological laws; on the contrary, he sees his dependence on his surroundings and looks for the laws of his development in that dependence."
"That's very interesting," said Metrov.

"What I really set out to write was a book on agriculture; but in studying the chief instrument of agriculture, the laborer," said Levin, reddening, "I couldn't help arriving at quite unexpected results."

And Levin began, cautiously, as though feeling his way, to lay out his views. He knew Metrov had written an article against the standard theory of political economy, but how far he could count on Metrov's sympathy with his own new views, he could not tell and could not read from the man's clever, untroubled face.
"And where, in your view, do the particular features of the Russian laborer lie?" Metrov asked. "In what one might call his biology — or in the conditions surrounding him?"

Levin saw that there was an idea behind this question that he did not agree with. But he went on explaining his own thought, that the Russian laborer has a quite particular view of the land, different from that of other peoples; and to back up the point he hurried to add that in his opinion this attitude of the Russian peasant came from his consciousness of a vocation to settle the vast empty stretches in the east.

"It's very easy to go wrong when you base any conclusion on the general vocation of a people," said Metrov, cutting Levin off. "The condition of the laborer will always depend on his relation to the land and to capital."
And without letting Levin finish setting out his idea, Metrov began explaining to him the particular point of his own theory.

What the point of Metrov's theory was, Levin did not understand, because he did not take the trouble to. He saw that Metrov, like other people, despite his own article attacking the current theory of political economy, still looked at the position of the Russian peasant simply from the standpoint of capital, wages, and rent. He would have had to admit that in the eastern — much the larger — part of Russia, rent was still zero; that for nine-tenths of the eighty million Russian peasants wages took the form simply of food they grew for themselves; and that capital scarcely existed except in the form of the most primitive tools. Yet it was only from that standpoint that he considered each laborer, although on many points he differed from the economists and had his own theory of the wage-fund, which he was now expounding to Levin.

Levin listened reluctantly and at first put up objections. He would have liked to interrupt Metrov, to spell out his own thought, which in his view would have made any further exposition of Metrov's theories unnecessary. But later, convinced that they saw the matter so differently that they could never come to understand each other, he stopped objecting at all and simply listened. Although by now what Metrov was saying held no interest for him, he still felt a certain satisfaction in listening to him. It flattered his vanity that such a learned man was explaining his ideas to him so eagerly, with such intensity and such confidence in Levin's grasp of the subject — sometimes with just a hint pointing him toward a whole side of the question. He gave himself credit for this, not realizing that Metrov, who had already gone over his theory again and again with all his close friends, talked about it with special eagerness to anyone new, and in general was eager to talk to anyone about anything that interested him, even when it was still unclear to himself.
"We're running late, though," said Katavasov, looking at his watch as soon as Metrov had finished his lecture.

"Yes — there's a meeting of the Society of Amateurs today to mark Svintitch's jubilee," said Katavasov, answering Levin's question. "Pyotr Ivanovitch and I were going. I promised to give an address on his work in zoology. Come along with us — it's very interesting."
"Yes, it is time to be off," said Metrov. "Come with us, and from there, if you'd like, come to my place. I'd very much like to hear about your work."
"Oh, no! It's not ready yet, it's unfinished. But I'll be very glad to come to the meeting."
"Listen, friends — have you heard? He has submitted the separate report," Katavasov called from the next room, where he was putting on his frock coat.

And a conversation broke out on the university question, which was one of the big events that winter in Moscow. Three older professors on the council had refused to back the opinion of the younger ones. The young ones had filed a separate resolution. In the view of some, this was monstrous; in the view of others it was the simplest and fairest thing to do — and the professors had split into two camps.

One side, the one Katavasov belonged to, saw in the other a contemptible betrayal and treachery, while the other side saw in them childishness and a lack of respect for the authorities. Although he was not part of the university, Levin had already heard and talked about the matter several times during his stay in Moscow, and had his own opinion. He joined in the conversation, which continued out in the street as all three of them walked to the buildings of the old university.

The meeting had already begun. Around the cloth-covered table where Katavasov and Metrov took their seats there were about half a dozen people, and one of them was bent close over a manuscript, reading something aloud. Levin sat down in one of the empty chairs that stood around the table and, in a whisper, asked a student next to him what was being read. The student looked at Levin with displeasure and said:
"Biography."
The biography was not something Levin cared about, but he could not stop himself from listening, and picked up a number of fresh, intriguing details about the life of this eminent man of science.

When the reader had finished, the chairman thanked him and read out some verses sent in by the poet Ment for the jubilee, then said a few words of thanks to the poet. Then Katavasov, in his loud, ringing voice, delivered his address on the scientific work of the man whose jubilee was being celebrated.

When Katavasov had finished, Levin looked at his watch, saw it was past one, and realized there would be no time before the concert to read Metrov his book — and in any case he no longer cared to. During the reading he had been turning over their earlier conversation. He saw clearly now that even if Metrov's ideas might have some value, his own ideas had a value too, and that their ideas could only be made clear and lead somewhere if each man worked on his own in his chosen direction — and that nothing would be gained by joining them together. Having decided to decline Metrov's invitation, Levin went up to him at the end of the meeting. Metrov introduced Levin to the chairman, with whom he was discussing the political news. Metrov told the chairman what he had already told Levin, and Levin made the same observations on the news that he had made earlier that morning, but for the sake of variety he added a new opinion that had only just occurred to him. After that the conversation turned again to the university question. Since Levin had heard it all already, he hurried to tell Metrov he was sorry he could not take advantage of his invitation, said good-bye, and drove off to Lvov's.

title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: Lvov — the husband of Kitty's sister Natalia — had passed his entire life in the capitals of foreign countries, where he was schooled and where he had served as a diplomat.

The previous year he had left the diplomatic service, not on account of any "unpleasantness" (he had never had any "unpleasantness" with anyone), and had been transferred to a department of the court of the palace in Moscow, in order to give his two boys the best possible education.
Despite the sharp contrast in their habits and views, and the fact that Lvov was older than Levin, they had seen a great deal of each other that winter and had taken a strong liking to each other.
Lvov was at home, and Levin went in to him unannounced.

Lvov, in a belted house coat and chamois leather slippers, was sitting in an armchair, and through a pince-nez with blue glasses he was reading a book that stood on a reading desk, holding in his beautiful hand a half-burned cigarette daintily away from himself.
His handsome, refined, still youthful-looking face — to which his curly, glistening silvery hair gave an even more aristocratic air — lit up with a smile when he saw Levin.

"Capital! I was just about to send for you. How's Kitty? Sit here, it's more comfortable." He stood up and pushed forward a rocking chair. "Have you read the latest circular in the _Journal de St. Pétersbourg?_ I think it's excellent," he said, with a slight French accent.

Levin told him what he had heard from Katavasov about what was being said in Petersburg, and after talking a little about politics, he told him about his meeting with Metrov and the learned society's session. Lvov was very interested.

"That's what I envy you for — being able to move in these interesting scientific circles," he said. And as he talked, he slipped, as usual, into French, which came easier to him. "It's true I have no time for it. My official work and the children leave me none; and then I'm not ashamed to admit that my own education was too patchy."

"I don't believe that," said Levin with a smile, touched, as he always was, by Lvov's low opinion of himself — which was in no way put on out of a wish to seem or to be modest, but was completely sincere.

"Oh, yes — really! I feel now how badly educated I am. To educate my children, I positively have to look up a great deal, and frankly to study myself. Because it's not enough to have teachers — there has to be someone to oversee them, just as on your land you need laborers and a foreman. Look at what I'm reading" — he pointed at Buslaev's _Grammar_ on the desk — "Misha is supposed to know this, and it's so difficult.... Here, explain it to me.... Here he says...."
Levin tried to explain that you couldn't understand it, you just had to be taught it; but Lvov would not agree with him.
"Oh, you're making fun of it!"
"On the contrary — you can't imagine how, when I look at you, I'm always studying the task ahead of me, namely the education of one's children."
"Well, there's nothing for you to learn," said Lvov.
"All I know," said Levin, "is that I've never seen children better brought up than yours, and I wouldn't wish for any better than yours."
Lvov visibly tried to hold back his delight, but he was positively beaming with smiles.
"As long as they end up better than me! That's all I ask. You don't realize yet what hard work it is," he said, "with boys who were left to grow up half-wild abroad like mine."
"You'll make all that up. They're such bright children. The main thing is the education of character. That's what I learn from watching your children."

"You talk about the education of character. You can't imagine how difficult that is! You've barely managed to fight off one bad tendency when others spring up, and the struggle starts again. If one didn't have a support in religion — remember we talked about that — no father could bring up children relying on his own strength alone, without that help."
This subject, which always interested Levin, was cut off by the entrance of the beautiful Natalia Alexandrovna, dressed to go out.

"I didn't know you were here," she said — clearly not regretful but positively pleased to be interrupting a conversation on a topic she had heard so much about that she was tired of it. "Well, how is Kitty? I'm dining with you today. Tell you what, Arseny," she turned to her husband, "you take the carriage."

And husband and wife began working out their plans for the day. Since the husband had to drive to meet someone on official business, while the wife had to go to the concert and to a public meeting of a committee on the Eastern Question, there was a great deal to settle. Levin had to take part in their plans as one of the family. It was agreed that Levin would go with Natalia to the concert and the meeting, and that from there they would send the carriage to the office for Arseny, who would call for Natalia and take her back to Kitty's — or, if he had not yet finished his work, he would send the carriage back and Levin would go with her.
"He spoils me," Lvov said to his wife. "He assures me our children are splendid, when I know how much that's bad there is in them."

"Arseny always goes to extremes, that's what I keep saying," said his wife. "If you look for perfection you'll never be satisfied. And it's true, as papa says — when we were being brought up there was one extreme, we were kept down in the basement while our parents lived in the best rooms; now it's just the opposite — the parents are in the wash house and the children are in the best rooms. Parents these days aren't expected to live at all, only to exist entirely for their children."
"Well, what if they prefer it that way?" Lvov said with his beautiful smile, touching her hand. "Anyone who didn't know you would think you were a stepmother and not a real mother."
"No, extremes aren't good in anything," Natalia said serenely, setting his paper-knife straight in its proper place on the table.

"Well, come on over here, my perfect children," Lvov said to the two handsome boys as they walked in; they bowed to Levin and then went up to their father, plainly with something they wanted to ask him.

Levin would have liked to talk to them, to hear what they would say to their father, but Natalia began talking to him, and then Lvov's colleague in the service, Mahotin, walked in in his court uniform to go with Lvov to meet someone, and conversation kept up without a break on Herzegovina, Princess Korzinskaya, the town council, and the sudden death of Madame Apraksina.
Levin even forgot the errand he had been entrusted with. He remembered it just as he was heading into the hall.
"Oh — Kitty asked me to talk to you about Oblonsky," he said, as Lvov was standing on the stairs seeing his wife and Levin off.
"Yes, yes — maman wants us, _les beaux-frères,_ to go after him," he said, blushing. "But why should I?"
"Well, then, I'll go after him," said Madame Lvova with a smile, standing in her white sheepskin cape, waiting for them to finish. "Come, let's go."

title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: At the concert that afternoon two very interesting pieces were performed. One was a fantasia, _King Lear;_ the other was a quartet dedicated to the memory of Bach. Both were new and in the new style, and Levin was eager to form an opinion of them. After seeing his sister-in-law to her seat, he stood against a column and tried to listen as attentively and conscientiously as he could. He tried not to let his attention be pulled away, and not to spoil his impression by looking at the conductor in his white tie, waving his arms — which always interfered so much with his enjoyment of music — or at the ladies in bonnets with the strings carefully tied over their ears, and all these people either thinking about nothing at all or thinking about every possible thing except the music. He tried to avoid running into musical experts or talkative acquaintances, and stood staring at the floor right in front of him, listening.

But the more he listened to the fantasia of _King Lear,_ the further he felt from forming any definite opinion of it. There was, as it were, a continual beginning, a preparation for some musical expression of feeling, and then it fell apart again immediately, breaking into new musical motifs — or into nothing but the composer's whims, sounds that were extremely complex but disconnected. And these fragmentary musical expressions, though sometimes beautiful, were unpleasant, because they came at you completely unexpectedly and were not led up to by anything. Cheerfulness and grief and despair and tenderness and triumph followed one another with no connection at all, like the emotions of a madman. And those emotions, like a madman's, sprang up out of nowhere.

Throughout the performance Levin felt like a deaf man watching people dance, and was in a state of complete bewilderment when the fantasia was over, and felt a great weariness from the fruitless strain on his attention. Loud applause broke out on all sides. Everyone stood up, milled about, started talking. Eager to throw some light on his own confusion using the impressions of others, Levin began walking around looking for connoisseurs, and was glad to see a well-known musical amateur talking with Pestsov, whom he knew.

"Marvelous!" Pestsov was saying in his mellow bass. "How are you, Konstantin Dmitrievitch? Particularly sculptural and plastic, so to speak, and richly colored is that passage where you feel Cordelia approaching — where woman, _das ewig Weibliche,_ comes into conflict with fate. Isn't it?"
"You mean ... what does Cordelia have to do with it?" Levin asked timidly, forgetting that the fantasia was supposed to depict King Lear.
"Cordelia comes in ... look here!" said Pestsov, tapping his finger on the satin surface of the program he was holding and handing it to Levin.
Only then did Levin remember the title of the fantasia, and he hurried to read in the Russian translation the lines from Shakespeare printed on the back of the program.
"You can't follow it without this," Pestsov said to Levin, since the person he had been talking to had walked off and he had no one else to talk to.

During the _entr'acte_ Levin and Pestsov fell into an argument about the merits and defects of music of the Wagner school. Levin held that the mistake of Wagner and all his followers was in trying to push music into the territory of another art, just as poetry goes wrong when it tries to paint a face the way painting is supposed to. As an example of this mistake he cited the sculptor who had carved in marble certain poetic phantoms hovering around the figure of a poet on a pedestal. "These phantoms were so far from being phantoms that they were positively clinging to the ladder," said Levin. The comparison pleased him, but then he could not remember whether he had used the same phrase before — and to Pestsov, too — and as he spoke it he felt awkward.
Pestsov maintained that art is one, and that it can reach its highest expressions only by joining together every kind of art.

The second piece on the program Levin could not really listen to. Pestsov, standing next to him, was talking to him almost the entire time, criticizing the music for its excessive, affected pretense of simplicity, and comparing it to the simplicity of the Pre-Raphaelites in painting. On the way out Levin ran into many more acquaintances, with whom he talked about politics, music, and people they both knew. Among others he met Count Bol, whom he had completely forgotten to call on.
"Well, go right now then," Madame Lvova said when he told her; "perhaps they won't be at home, and then you can come to the meeting to fetch me. You'll still find me there."

title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: "Maybe they're not at home?" said Levin as he stepped into the hall of Countess Bola's house.
"They are; please go in," said the porter, briskly taking his overcoat off him.
"How annoying!" Levin thought with a sigh, peeling off one glove and smoothing his hat. "What did I come for? What have I got to say to them?"

Passing through the first drawing room, Levin met Countess Bola in the doorway as she was giving an order to a servant, her face careworn and severe. Seeing Levin she smiled and asked him to come into the little drawing room, where he could hear voices. In that room two of the countess's daughters were sitting in armchairs along with a Moscow colonel Levin knew. Levin walked up, greeted them, and sat down beside the sofa with his hat on his knees.
"How is your wife? Were you at the concert? We couldn't go. Mamma had to be at the funeral service."
"Yes, I heard.... What a sudden death!" said Levin.
The countess came in, sat down on the sofa, and she too asked about his wife and the concert.
Levin answered and repeated a question about Madame Apraksina's sudden death.
"But she had always been in poor health."
"Were you at the opera yesterday?"
"Yes, I was."
"Lucca was very good."

"Yes, very good," he said, and since it was entirely unimportant to him what they thought of him, he began repeating what they had heard a hundred times about the special qualities of the singer's talent. Countess Bola pretended to be listening. Then, when he had said enough and paused, the colonel — who had been quiet up to that point — began to speak. The colonel too talked about the opera, and about culture. At last, after going on about the proposed _folle journée_ at Turin's, the colonel laughed, stood up noisily, and left. Levin stood up too, but saw from the countess's face that it was not yet time for him to go. He had to stay two minutes longer. He sat down again.
But since he was thinking the whole time about how stupid this all was, he could not come up with a topic of conversation, and sat in silence.
"You're not going to the public meeting? They say it's going to be very interesting," the countess began.
"No, I promised my _belle-sœur_ to fetch her from it," Levin said.
A silence followed. The mother once more exchanged glances with one of the daughters.
"Well, now I think the time has come," Levin thought, and he stood up. The ladies shook hands with him and asked him to say _mille choses_ to his wife from them.
The porter, as he handed him his coat, asked, "Where is your honor staying?" and immediately wrote down his address in a large, handsomely bound book.

"It doesn't really matter to me, of course, but I still feel embarrassed and terribly foolish," Levin thought, comforting himself with the idea that this was simply what everyone did. He set off for the public meeting, where his sister-in-law was waiting so they could drive home together.

At the public meeting of the committee there were a great many people, and almost all of the highest society. Levin arrived in time for the report, which, as everyone said, was very interesting. When the reading of the report was over, people moved around, and Levin met Sviazhsky, who pressed him very hard to come that evening to a meeting of the Society of Agriculture, where a celebrated lecture was to be given; and Stepan Arkadyevitch, who had only just come from the races; and many other acquaintances. Levin heard and made various comments on the meeting, on the new fantasia, and on a public trial. But, probably from the mental fatigue he was beginning to feel, he made a blunder in talking about the trial, and this blunder he remembered several times afterwards with annoyance. Speaking of the sentence handed down on a foreigner who had been condemned in Russia, and of how unfair it would be to punish him by exile abroad, Levin repeated something he had heard the day before in conversation from an acquaintance.

"I think sending him abroad is much the same as punishing a carp by putting it back in the water," Levin said. Then he remembered that this idea, which he had heard from an acquaintance and put forward as his own, came from a fable of Krilov's, and that the acquaintance had picked it up from a newspaper article.
After driving home with his sister-in-law and finding Kitty in good spirits and quite well, Levin drove on to the club.

title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Levin arrived at the club at exactly the right moment. Members and guests were pulling up just as he did. He had not been to the club in a long time—not since his Moscow days when he was finishing up at the university and starting to go out in society. He remembered the place itself, the layout and small details, but he had completely forgotten the feeling it used to give him. The moment he drove into the wide semicircular court, climbed down from the sledge, and walked up the steps; the moment the hall porter, sash slung crosswise over his chest, silently bowed and opened the door; the moment he caught sight of the porter's room with its piled cloaks and galoshes, left by members who would rather not deal with them upstairs; the moment he heard the strange bell announcing his arrival as he went up the easy, carpeted staircase, saw the statue on the landing, and met the third porter at the upper doors—an older but familiar figure in club livery, opening the door at an unhurried pace and giving each arrival a glance—the old feeling came back in a wave: a sense of ease, comfort, and propriety.

"Your hat, please," the porter said to Levin, who had forgotten the rule about leaving hats downstairs. "Long while since you've been. The prince put your name down yesterday. Prince Stepan Arkadyevitch isn't here yet."
The porter knew not only Levin but the whole network of his connections, and he mentioned his close friends right away.

Walking through the outer hall, divided up by screens, and past the small partitioned room on the right where a man tended the fruit buffet, Levin passed an old gentleman shuffling slowly forward and stepped into the dining-room, which was full of noise and people.

He walked between the tables—nearly all of them taken—and looked around at the diners. There were people of every kind, old and young, some he barely knew, others close friends. Not a single face looked harried or worried. Everyone seemed to have left their cares and anxieties in the porter's room along with their hats, all of them deliberately settling in to enjoy the material pleasures of life. Sviazhsky was there, and Shtcherbatsky, Nevyedovsky, the old prince, Vronsky, and Sergey Ivanovitch.
"Ah! What kept you?" the prince said, smiling, and reaching back over his shoulder to give Levin his hand. "How's Kitty?" he added, smoothing the napkin he had tucked under his waistcoat buttons.
"All right; the three of them are dining at home."
"Ah, the 'Aline-Nadine' party, of course! No room with us. Go over to that table and grab a seat, quick," said the prince, then turned away and carefully accepted a plate of eel soup.

"Levin, over here!" a friendly voice called from farther on. It was Turovtsin. He was sitting with a young officer, and two chairs beside them were turned upside down. Levin went over gladly. He had always liked Turovtsin, the good-natured rake—he was tied in his mind to memories of his courtship—and just now, after the strain of intellectual talk, the sight of Turovtsin's easy face was particularly welcome.
"For you and Oblonsky. He'll be here any minute."
The young man, sitting very straight, his eyes glinting with permanent amusement, was an officer from Petersburg named Gagin. Turovtsin introduced them.
"Oblonsky's always late."
"Ah, here he is!"
"You only just got here?" said Oblonsky, walking quickly over. "Good day. Had your vodka? Well, come on then."

Levin got up and went with him to the long table laid out with spirits and appetizers of every kind. You would think two dozen delicacies would offer something to anyone's taste, but Stepan Arkadyevitch asked for something particular, and one of the liveried waiters standing by promptly brought it. They each took a glass and went back to their table.

Right away, while they were still on the soup, Gagin was served champagne and told the waiter to fill four glasses. Levin didn't refuse the wine, and called for a second bottle.
